# Why we need FDA? {background-color="#1e3a5f"}

---

## The data we actually have



Some of the most important data sources in health sciences are **not really vectors of numbers** — they are curves:

::: {.fragment}
- **Growth trajectories** — height over age from birth to adulthood
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Wearable sensor signals** — accelerometry, heart rate, glucose monitors
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Longitudinal biomarker profiles** — CD4 counts, PSA, cortisol curves
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Gene expression time courses** — RNA-seq over developmental stages
:::

::: {.fragment}

- **Neuroimaging signals** — EEG, fMRI BOLD time series

:::

::: {.fragment}

> These are not vectors — they are discrete samples of an underlying continuous function.

:::


::: {.notes}
The key point here is motivational. The audience needs to feel the problem before any methodology. These data types are familiar to any health researcher — the question is what goes wrong when we use standard multivariate or longitudinal methods.

The question is: what happens when we try to analyze them with standard multivariate or longitudinal methods? Why we need the FDA approach? The next three slides show three concrete failure modes.
:::

---

## Problem 1: the exchangeability trap

> What happens when we treat a curve as a vector?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}

**Setting:** childhood height measured at ages 2, 5, 8, 12, 16

**Multivariate approach:** treat each age as a separate variable

::: {.fragment}

**Problems:**

- The covariance matrix $\Sigma$ depends entirely on **which ages were chosen** — two studies with different measurement schedules are incomparable

:::

::: {.fragment}
- Biological features (pubertal growth spurt) are **invisible**

:::

::: {.fragment}

- Permuting ages leaves multivariate analysis unchanged — but completely destroys the biological meaning

:::

:::


:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r fig-discretization}
#| fig-height: 5
data("growth")
ages  <- growth$age
girls <- growth$hgtf

tb_g <- as_tibble(girls) |>
  mutate(age = ages) |>
  pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "subject", values_to = "height")


set.seed(1)
sel_ages <- c(2, 5, 8, 12, 16)
sel_idx  <- sapply(sel_ages, function(a) which.min(abs(ages - a)))

# show 8 individual girls
idx_girls <- c(1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50)

tb_sel <- as_tibble(girls[, idx_girls]) |>
  mutate(age = ages) |>
  pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "subject", values_to = "height")

tb_pts <- as_tibble(girls[sel_idx, idx_girls]) |>
  mutate(age = sel_ages) |>
  pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "subject", values_to = "height")

ggplot(tb_sel, aes(age, height, group = subject, color = subject)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.7, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = tb_pts, aes(age, height),
             size = 4, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sel_ages, linetype = "dotted",
             color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  annotate("text", x = 12, y = 85,
           label = "Observed\ntime points", color = "grey30",
           size = 4.5, hjust = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "The discretization trap",
       subtitle = "Dots = what multivariate analysis sees. Lines = what actually exists.",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_fda()
```

:::
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## The core issue
The **ordering** and **continuity** of time are ignored. FDA treats the measurement schedule as what it is: a sampling design.
:::


::: {.notes}


The key insight is that the measurement schedule is a design choice, not a
property of the data. A child's height exists continuously — we just happen
to measure it at 5 time points. Multivariate analysis treats those 5 numbers
as 5 separate variables with no particular ordering. FDA treats them as
5 noisy observations of a single continuous curve.

This has an immediate practical consequence: two studies that measured at
different ages cannot be directly compared in the multivariate framework.
In the functional framework, both estimate the same underlying curve C(s,t)
and are directly comparable.

Mixed models do respect temporal ordering — but they impose a 
**parametric mean** and a **parametric covariance structure**.
FDA estimates both non-parametrically, directly from the data.
The measurement schedule remains a design choice, not a constraint
on what can be estimated.

:::

---

## Problem 2: the rigid model trap

> What happens when we impose a parametric mean structure?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="51%"}

::: {style="font-size: 73%;"}

**Setting:** CD4 cell counts in HIV patients *(Zeger & Diggle, 1994)*.

**Linear mixed model approach:** assume a parametric mean trajectory — linear or quadratic in time.

$$\mu(t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 t^2$$

::: {.fragment}

**Problems:**

- A parabola has **exactly one turning point** — but the true trajectory may decline, plateau, rebound, or decline

:::

::: {.fragment}
- The variance structure is assumed **constant** ($\sigma^2 \quad$) or AR(1) — cannot detect that variability is higher at certain stages of disease

:::

::: {.fragment}

- Clinically meaningful features — **time to nadir**, **rate of decline pre-treatment**, **rebound after ART** — are invisible or distorted

:::

:::

:::

::: {.column width="49%"}

```{r fig-rigid-model}
#| fig-height: 7.5

set.seed(42)
t_hiv <- seq(0, 36, length.out = 50)
n_hiv <- 40

# Simulate realistic CD4 trajectories: decline then partial recovery
sim_cd4 <- function(i) {
  nadir_t   <- runif(1, 10, 20)
  nadir_val <- runif(1, 100, 300)
  baseline  <- runif(1, 600, 900)
  recovery  <- runif(1, 0.3, 0.8)
  baseline * exp(-0.08 * t_hiv) +
    nadir_val * (1 - exp(-0.2 * abs(t_hiv - nadir_t))) * recovery +
    rnorm(length(t_hiv), 0, 20)
}

cd4_mat <- sapply(1:n_hiv, sim_cd4)
cd4_df  <- as.data.frame(cd4_mat) |>
  setNames(paste0("s", 1:n_hiv)) |>
  mutate(time = t_hiv) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "subject", values_to = "cd4")

# Fit quadratic mean
lm_fit   <- lm(cd4 ~ poly(time, 2), data = cd4_df)
pred_df  <- tibble(time = t_hiv,
                   quad = predict(lm_fit, newdata = tibble(time = t_hiv)),
                   true = rowMeans(cd4_mat))

ggplot(cd4_df, aes(time, cd4, group = subject)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.18, color = "#1e3a5f", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = pred_df, aes(time, quad, group = 1),
            color = "#e9c46a", linewidth = 1.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = pred_df, aes(time, true, group = 1),
            color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 30, y = 750,
           label = "Quadratic fit", color = "#e9c46a",
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 30, y = 680,
           label = "True mean curve", color = "#e63946",
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) +
  labs(title = "The rigid model trap",
       subtitle = "CD4 count trajectories — HIV patients (simulated)",
       x = "Months since diagnosis", y = "CD4 count (cells/mm3)") +
  theme_fda()
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}

CD4+ T-cells are a type of white blood cell that plays a central role in the immune response. HIV specifically targets and destroys CD4+ cells, so their count (measured in cells/mm³) is the primary clinical marker of disease progression. A healthy count is 500–1500 cells/mm³. As HIV progresses untreated, CD4 count falls — below 200 cells/mm³ is the threshold for AIDS diagnosis. With antiretroviral therapy (ART), CD4 count partially recovers. The trajectory of CD4 over time — its rate of decline, time to nadir, and post-treatment rebound — is far more informative than any single measurement, which is exactly why it is a canonical example for FDA: the clinically meaningful information lives in the shape of the curve, not in a scalar summary.

The quadratic mean is shown in yellow — it captures the general downward trend
but completely misses the heterogeneity in individual trajectories. Some patients
decline fast and recover, others decline slowly without recovery, others show
biphasic patterns. These clinically meaningful differences are invisible to a
model that forces everyone onto the same parabola.

FDA estimates the mean curve non-parametrically — it follows the data rather
than imposing a shape. And it estimates the covariance surface C(s,t) freely,
which reveals that variability is much higher at certain stages of disease
progression than at others.
:::

---

## Problem 3: the signal is in the shape

> What happens when we summarize a curve to a scalar?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {style="font-size: 71%;"}

**Setting:** physical activity measured by accelerometry — NHANES substudy *(Leroux et al., 2019)*.

**Standard approach:** summarize to total activity count per day — one number per subject.

::: {.fragment}

**The problem:** two subjects with **identical total activity** can have completely different daily patterns:

- One is active in the morning, sedentary in the afternoon
- The other is sedentary in the morning, active in the evening

:::

::: {.fragment}

**Clinically, these are different phenotypes:**

- Circadian disruption
- Frailty patterns
- Sleep disorders
- Metabolic risk profiles

The scalar summary discards exactly the information that matters.
:::

:::

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{r fig-actigraphy}
#| fig-height: 7.5

set.seed(99)
hours <- seq(0, 24, length.out = 200)

# Subject A: morning active
subj_A <- 2 * dnorm(hours, mean = 9,  sd = 2) * 100 +
           1 * dnorm(hours, mean = 14, sd = 1) * 100 +
           rnorm(200, 0, 0.8)
subj_A <- pmax(subj_A, 0)

# Subject B: evening active — same total
subj_B <- 1.5 * dnorm(hours, mean = 18, sd = 2) * 100 +
          1.2 * dnorm(hours, mean = 20, sd = 1.5) * 100 +
          rnorm(200, 0, 0.8)
subj_B <- pmax(subj_B, 0)

# Scale so totals are equal
subj_B <- subj_B * (sum(subj_A) / sum(subj_B))

act_df <- bind_rows(
  tibble(hour = hours, activity = subj_A, subject = "Morning-active (A)"),
  tibble(hour = hours, activity = subj_B, subject = "Evening-active (B)")
)

ggplot(act_df, aes(hour, activity, color = subject, fill = subject)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.25, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#e63946", "#2a9d8f"), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = c("#e63946", "#2a9d8f"), name = NULL) +
  annotate("text", x = 12, y = max(subj_A) * 1.1,
           label = "Same total activity count\nCompletely different shapes",
           color = "#0f1f3d", size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "The aggregation trap",
       subtitle = "Accelerometry — simulated daily activity profiles",
       x = "Hour of day", y = "Activity (counts/min)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Reference: Leroux et al. (2019), Statistics in Biosciences; Goldsmith et al. (2016), JASA.

This is perhaps the most intuitive failure mode for a clinical audience.
The total activity count is the most commonly reported summary in
accelerometry studies — steps per day, activity counts per day. But
it discards all temporal information.

FDA treats the 24-hour activity profile as a single functional observation.
The mean function tells you the typical daily pattern. The covariance
surface tells you at which hours people differ most. FPCA reveals
phenotypes — morning-active vs evening-active vs uniformly sedentary —
that are invisible in any scalar summary.

Leroux et al. (2019) showed that functional predictors from accelerometry
outperform scalar summaries in predicting mortality and chronic disease,
precisely because the shape of the activity curve contains clinical
information beyond the total.
:::

---

## What Changes?

::: {style="font-size: 78%;"}


| | Multivariate | Mixed effects / Longitudinal | FDA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit of observation | Vector $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$ | Vector at fixed time points | Function $x_i(t) \in L^2(T)$ |
| Mean structure | $\bar{\mathbf{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ | Parametric $\mu(t) = \mathbf{z}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$ | Non-parametric $\mu(t)$ — estimated freely |
| Covariance structure | $p \times p$ matrix $\Sigma$ | Parametric: AR(1), compound symmetry... | Surface $C(s,t)$ — estimated freely |
| Temporal ordering | ❌ Ignored — coordinates exchangeable | ✅ Respected via parametric structure | ✅ Respected via smoothness assumption |
| Measurement schedule | Defines the data | Defines the data | Just a sampling design |
| Between-study comparability | ❌ Depends on which variables measured | ❌ Depends on measurement times | ✅ $C(s,t)$ is a process property |
| Derivative inference | ❌ Not possible | ❌ Not possible | ✅ $x_i'(t)$, $x_i''(t)$ are objects |
| Dimensionality reduction | PCA in $\mathbb{R}^p$ | Not standard | FPCA — optimal basis from data |
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The key longitudinal vs FDA distinction
Mixed models ask: *"what is the average trajectory and how do subjects deviate from it — within a parametric family?"*
FDA asks: *"what is the actual shape of the mean curve, how does variability evolve over time, and what modes of variation exist in the sample?"*
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide to come back to when someone asks "why not just use a mixed model?". The answer has three parts.

First, the mean: a mixed model forces the mean trajectory into a parametric family (linear, quadratic, spline with fixed knots) — FDA estimates it freely. 

Second, the covariance: a mixed model assumes a parametric correlation structure (AR(1), compound symmetry, unstructured but finite) — FDA estimates C(s,t) as a full surface.

Third, the measurement schedule: in a mixed model, the timepoints you chose partly define your model; in FDA they are just a sampling design and C(s,t) is a property of the process, not of your study design.

The sparse/irregular caveat: for very sparse longitudinal data (3-5 obs per subject), pure FDA requires PACE methods — mixed models are more natural there.
:::

---


## Curse of dimensionality?

> Does FDA solve the Curse of Dimensionality? Counterintuitively — yes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}

**The curse in multivariate analysis:**

With $p$ variables and $n$ observations, data matrix is $n \times p$. As $p \to \infty \quad$:

- The sample covariance matrix $\widehat{\Sigma}\quad$ ($p \times p \quad$) becomes **singular or poorly estimated** — you need $n \gg p$
- Distances become meaningless — all points equidistant in high dimensions
- PCA needs $n > p$ for a well-defined solution

**How FDA avoids it:**

FDA does not estimate a $p \times p$ matrix. It estimates a **smooth surface** $C(s,t)$ — using the fact that nearby time points are correlated. The smoothness assumption drastically reduces the effective number of parameters.
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r fig-curse}
#| fig-height: 9

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

# ── Panel 1: rank deficiency of sample cov matrix as p grows ─────────────────
set.seed(1)
n_subj <- 80
ps     <- c(10, 30, 50, 80, 100, 150, 200, 300, 500)

rank_df <- map_dfr(ps, function(p) {
  # Simulate functional data: smooth curves sampled at p points
  t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = p)
  # Generate from a smooth process (low intrinsic dim)
  scores <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj * 5), n_subj, 5)
  basis  <- sapply(1:5, function(k) sin(k * pi * t_grid))
  X      <- scores %*% t(basis) + matrix(rnorm(n_subj * p, 0, 0.1), n_subj, p)
  Sigma  <- cov(X)
  eigs   <- eigen(Sigma, only.values = TRUE)$values
  eff_rank <- sum(eigs > 1e-8)
  tibble(
    p         = p,
    eff_rank  = eff_rank,
    ratio     = eff_rank / p,
    singular  = p > n_subj
  )
})

p1 <- ggplot(rank_df, aes(p, eff_rank)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1e3a5f", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(color = singular), size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = n_subj, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#e63946", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#2a9d8f", "TRUE" = "#e63946"),
                     labels = c("FALSE" = "Full rank", "TRUE" = "Rank deficient"),
                     name = NULL) +
  annotate("text", x = n_subj + 6, y = 15,
           label = paste0("p = n = ", n_subj),
           color = "#e63946", size = 6, hjust = 0) +
  labs(title    = "Effective rank of sample covariance",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", n_subj, " subjects — rank deficient when p > n"),
       x = "Number of time points p", y = "Effective rank") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# ── Panel 2: FPCA reduces to K << p dimensions ───────────────────────────────
set.seed(2)
p_large <- 300
t_grid  <- seq(0, 1, length.out = p_large)
K_true  <- 4

# Smooth functional data with K_true intrinsic dimensions
basis_true <- sapply(1:K_true, function(k) sin(k * pi * t_grid))
scores_true <- matrix(rnorm(n_subj * K_true, 0,
                             c(3, 2, 1.2, 0.8)), n_subj, K_true)
X_large <- scores_true %*% t(basis_true) +
           matrix(rnorm(n_subj * p_large, 0, 0.15), n_subj, p_large)

bs_cd  <- fda::create.bspline.basis(rangeval = c(0,1), nbasis = 20, norder = 4)
fdp_cd <- fda::fdPar(bs_cd, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-3)
fd_cd  <- fda::smooth.basis(t_grid, t(X_large), fdp_cd)$fd
fpca_cd <- fda::pca.fd(fd_cd, nharm = 10)

pve_cd <- cumsum(fpca_cd$varprop) * 100

scree_cd <- tibble(k = 1:10, pve = pve_cd)

p2 <- ggplot(scree_cd, aes(k, pve)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2a9d8f", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(color = "#2a9d8f", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 95, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#e63946", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y = 93,
           label = "95% variance explained", color = "#e63946",
           size = 3.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = K_true, xend = K_true,
           y = 0, yend = pve_cd[K_true],
           color = "#1e3a5f", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = K_true + 0.3, y = 30,
           label = paste0("K = ", K_true, "\n(true dim)"),
           color = "#1e3a5f", size = 3.5, hjust = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(title    = "FPCA recovers intrinsic dimensionality",
       subtitle = paste0("p = ", p_large, " time points → K = ",
                         K_true, " components explain >95% variance"),
       x = "Number of components K", y = "Cumulative variance explained (%)") +
  theme_fda()

p1 # / p2 + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1))
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the clean answer to "but doesn't high-dimensional data always cause problems?". In multivariate analysis, yes — when p > n the covariance matrix is rank-deficient and PCA is undefined or unstable. FDA avoids this by never estimating a p x p matrix. It estimates a smooth surface C(s,t) using the structural assumption that nearby time points are correlated — which radically reduces the effective number of parameters regardless of p. FPCA then finds the intrinsic dimensionality K of the data — typically K is 3-5 even when p is in the hundreds. 

The left panel shows that once p > n, the sample covariance becomes rank-deficient.

The right panel shows that FPCA on the same data correctly identifies K = 4 intrinsic dimensions, explaining >95% of variance, regardless of p being 300.
:::


# What is FDA? {background-color="#1e3a5f"}

From vectors to functions 


---

## What is Functional Data Analysis?

::: {.notes}

The term was coined by Ramsay & Dalzell (1991). The foundational textbook is Ramsay & Silverman (2005), still the central reference.

What is NOT FDA: having many variables does not make it FDA. What defines FDA is that observations are intrinsically functional — there is a continuous underlying process of which the discrete data are a noisy sample.
We have just seen examples where treating curves as vectors or as parametric longitudinal profiles lost clinically relevant information. The natural question is: what statistical framework actually respects the nature of this data?
The answer is FDA. The idea is conceptually simple but has profound consequences: instead of observing a vector of p numbers per subject, we observe a function — a curve defined over a continuous domain (time, frequency, space...) — of which we only see p snapshots.

This is not just a notational change. It is a change of statistical space: from working in R^p

Rp to working in a function space — typically a Hilbert space of square-integrable functions, L2. That shift has implications for how we define mean, variance, distance, projection — everything.
:::

> Each observation is a function, not a vector.


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**The classical statistical unit:**

$$\mathbf{x}_i = (x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \ldots, x_{ip}) \in \mathbb{R}^p, \quad i=1,\ldots,n$$

A finite-dimensional vector. Our data lives in $\mathbb{R}^p$.


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The FDA Shift

The *unit of observation* is a **FUNCTION**: where multivariate analysis sees p variables, FDA sees p snapshots of a single continuous process. Each subject $i$ contributes **one curve** $X_i(t)$.
:::


:::
:::

. . .

**The functional statistical unit:**

$$X_i(t), \quad t \in T \subseteq \mathbb{R}, \quad i=1,\ldots,n$$

A curve defined over a continuous domain. Inference lives in an **infinite-dimensional space**.


> «The data are functions, and the methods of analysis must respect this»
> — Ramsay & Silverman, Functional Data Analysis (2005).

---

## Why does the space matter?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
Once we commit to a function space, we must **redefine everything**:

| Concept | $\mathbb{R}^p$ | Function space |
|---------|--------------|----------------|
| Mean | $\bar{\mathbf{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ a vector | $\mu(t)$, a curve |
| Covariance | $p \times p$ matrix | $C(s,t)$ (surface) |
| Distance | Euclidean $\|\cdot\|_2$ | $\int [x(t)-y(t)]^2 dt$ |
| PCA | Eigenvectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$ | Eigenfunctions |

Changing the space changes what **questions you can ask**.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r fig-shift}
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "An example of FDA"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
data("growth")
library(tidyverse)
ages <- growth$age
girls <- growth$hgtf # 54 girls

tb_curves <-
  as_tibble(girls) |>
  mutate("age" = ages) |>
  pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "subject", values_to = "height")

ggplot(tb_curves, aes(age, height, group = subject)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.25, color = "#1e3a5f", linewidth = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean,
               geom = "line", color = "#e63946",
               linewidth = 1.6, linetype = "solid") +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = 130,
           label = "μ(t): mean curve", color = "#e63946",
           hjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  labs(title = "Berkeley Growth Study",
       subtitle = "Subsample of 54 girls (from age 1 to 18). Each curve (function) is one observation",
       x = "Age (t in years)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_fda()
```
:::
:::

---

## Where do our data (curves) lives?

The choice of functional space has **direct consequences** for inference and what tools apply.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}


### $L^2(T)$ — Square-integrable functions

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
$L^2$ (**Hilbert space**) is the $\infty$-dimensional analogue of $\mathbb{R}^p$.


$$L^2(T) = \left\{ x(t): \int_{T} x(t)^2 \, dt < \infty \right\}$$

**Inner product**: $\langle x, y \rangle_{L^2} = \int_T x(t) y(t)dt$

✅ Supports FPCA, (functional) regression, projections (coordinates, orthonormal bases, etc)  

⚠️ Does **not** guarantee continuity or differentiability.

:::

::: {.fragment}

### $W^{m,2}(T)$ — Sobolev spaces

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}

m derivatives are also living in $L^2$:

$$W^{m,2}(T) = \left\{ x \in L^2: x^{(1)}, \ldots, x^{(m)} \in L^2 \right\}$$

✅ Supports derivative inference (velocity, acceleration)  


:::

:::

::: {.notes}

the L2 norm measures global energy — the area between two curves. But our observations are pointwise: we record x(t1),x(t2),…x(t_1), x(t_2), \ldots
x(t1​),x(t2​),… at specific time points. Two subjects whose curves are nearly identical in L2L^2
L2 norm could still show very different observed values, depending on when we measured them. In an RKHS, the norm directly controls pointwise behavior: small norm implies small values everywhere. This makes the space statistically coherent with how functional data are actually collected.

La distinción que vale la pena mantener es:

L2L^2
L2 mide
energía global — lo que ocurre en un conjunto de medida cero (un punto) no afecta a la norma
RKHS mide algo que sí controla lo puntual — por eso es el espacio natural cuando tus datos son muestras en puntos

✅ $W^{2,2}$ functions in $\mathbb{R}$ are continuous


:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


```{r}
t <- seq(0.000001, 1, length.out = 500)
set.seed(12345)
f_l2 <- sin(2 * pi * t) +
  ifelse(t > 0.25 & t < 0.255, 2.5, 0) +
  ifelse(t > 0.55 & t < 0.552, -2, 0) +
  ifelse(t > 0.78 & t < 0.782, 1.8, 0) +
  0.15 * rnorm(length(t))
f_sob <- 1.2 * sin(2*pi*t) +
    0.4 * sin(6*pi*t) +
    0.15 * sin(10*pi*t)
f_banach <- abs(t)^(-0.5)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 7
ggplot(tibble("t" = t, "f" = f_l2, "type" = "Hilbert (square-integrable)") |> 
         bind_rows(tibble("t" = t, "f" = f_sob, "type" = "Sobolev (m = 2)"))) +
  geom_line(aes(x = t, y = f, color = type),
            alpha = 0.75, linewidth = 1.7) +
  MetBrewer::scale_color_met_d(palette_name = "Renoir") +
  labs(title = "Curves living in Hilbert and Sobolev spaces",
       x = "t", y = "x(t)") +
  theme_fda()
```

:::

:::


---

## Where do our data (curves) lives?

| Space | Key property | Norm / inner product | Typical use in FDA |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|--------------------|
| $L^2(T)$ | Square-integrable | $\int x(t)y(t)\,dt$ | FPCA, functional regression |
| $W^{m,2}(T)$ | $m$ derivatives in $L^2$ | $L^2$ norm + derivatives | Penalized smoothing, derivative inference |
| $C(T),\, C^k(T)$ | Continuous / $k$-smooth | Supremum norm | Depth measures, hypothesis testing |
| RKHS | Pointwise evaluation bounded | Kernel-induced | Regularized regression, kernel FDA |

<br>

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
**In practice**, most FDA software assumes $L^2$ or Sobolev structure implicitly. Being explicit about the space is not pedantry: **it determines what questions you can legitimately ask of your data.**
:::

---

## When is it FDA? Three conditions

::: {.notes}

What is NOT FDA: having many variables does not make it FDA. What defines FDA is that observations are intrinsically functional — there is a continuous underlying process of which the discrete data are a noisy sample.

A practical question that always comes up: when is FDA justified over longitudinal or multivariate methods? Three conditions work as a guide:

1. Continuity of the underlying process. The phenomenon is continuous in its domain. Blood pressure does not jump discretely between measurements — a continuous process exists of which we only observe points. If the underlying process is genuinely discrete, FDA does not apply.

2. Local dependence structure (smoothness). Nearby observations are more similar than distant ones — there is a correlation structure that depends on proximity. This is not just a computational convenience: it is a substantive assumption about the biology. Glucose at 10:00 predicts glucose at 10:05 far better than at 18:00. Standard multivariate methods ignore this ordering; FDA exploits it.

+3. The whole curve is the inferential object. We are not interested in the value at a specific time point, nor in a scalar summary (mean, AUC, slope). We want to make inference on the complete function — its shape, variability, derivatives, local features. If the scientific question can be answered with a scalar summary, you do not need FDA.

Grey zone — sparse longitudinal data: with 3–5 measurements per subject you cannot reliably estimate one function per subject. PACE methods (Yao, Müller & Wang, JASA 2005) handle this by borrowing strength across subjects via the population covariance structure — FDA adapted to the clinical reality of many studies.
:::


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
A practical checklist before committing to a FDA framework:


::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}

::: {.fragment}
**1. Continuity of the underlying process**  
The phenomenon is continuous in its domain. **Blood pressure** does not jump discretely between observations (a continuous process exists).

:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}

**2. Local dependence structure (smoothness)**  
Nearby observations are more similar than distant ones. **Glucose** at 10:00 predicts glucose at 10:05 far better than at 18:00. This ordering is *structural*, not accidental — FDA exploits it; multivariate ignore it.

:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}

**3. The curve itself is the inferential object**  
We want to make inference on the *whole function* — its shape, derivatives, local features — not on a scalar summary (mean, AUC, slope).  

:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="35%"}
::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Grey zone: sparse longitudinal data
If you have 3–5 observations per subject, you **cannot** reliably estimate one function per subject. **Solution:** PACE methods *(Yao, Müller & Wang, JASA 2005)*

:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## What is NOT FDA
Having many variables or repeated measurements is not FDA.  

What defines FDA is the commitment that the **data-generating process is a continuous function**
:::
:::
:::

---

## The functional mean $\mu(t)$ {.center}

::: {.notes}

Conceptually it is the same operation — we average coordinate by coordinate — but now there are infinitely many coordinates, one per tt
t. The mean is not a number or a finite vector. It is a curve.*

*Why does this matter? Because the functional mean captures the typical shape of the process, not just its level. In growth curves, μ(t)\mu(t)
μ(t) tells you the average height trajectory as a function of age — including the inflection of the pubertal growth spurt. A longitudinal model with a parametric mean (linear, quadratic) gives you an approximation; FDA gives you the actual shape, estimated directly from the data.*

*The key visual:
n individual curves in translucent grey, with μ(t)
μ(t) overlaid as a bold curve. It should be immediately clear that μ(t)\mu(t)
μ(t) has its own shape — it is not a straight line.*

:::
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {style="font-size: 90%;"}

**Multivariate mean:** average over $n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$

$$\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$$

One number per variable: $p$ independent values. **Coordinates are exchangeable**.

<br>

::: {.fragment}

**Functional mean:** average over $n$ functions pointwise

$$\mu(t) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(t), \quad t \in T$$

**A curve** — evaluated at every $t$. Infinitely many "coordinates", one per $t$. The mean encodes the **typical shape** of the process —  including inflections, acceleration phases.

:::

:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 14
boys <- growth$hgtm 
mu_t_boys <- rowMeans(boys)
mu_t_girls <- rowMeans(girls)

tb_curves <-
  as_tibble(girls) |>
  mutate("age" = ages) |>
  pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "subject", values_to = "height") |> 
  mutate("sex" = "female") |> 
  bind_rows(as_tibble(boys) |>
              mutate("age" = ages) |>
              pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "subject", values_to = "height") |> 
              mutate("sex" = "male"))

tb_mean <-
  tibble("age" = ages, "mu" = mu_t_boys, "sex" = "male") |> 
  bind_rows(tibble("age" = ages, "mu" = mu_t_girls,
                   "sex" = "female"))
gg1 <-
  ggplot(tb_curves) +
  geom_line(aes(x = age, y = height, color = sex, group = subject),
            alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = tb_mean, aes(x = age, y = mu, color = sex, group = sex),
            linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#1e3a5f", "#e63946")) +
  annotate("text", x = 7, y = 170,
           label = "μ(t) (male)", color = "#e63946",
           fontface = "bold", size = 6) +
  annotate("text", x = 12.5, y = 120,
           label = "μ(t) (male)", color = "#1e3a5f",
           fontface = "bold", size = 6) +
  annotate("segment", x = 16, xend = 16,
           y = 135, yend = 175,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2,"cm")),
           color = "grey40", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = 120,
           label = "Pubertal growth\nspurt in males",
           color = "grey30", size = 5, hjust = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Functional mean of height trajectories",
       subtitle = "Berkeley Growth Study",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_fda()
gg2 <-
  ggplot(tb_curves |> 
         left_join(tb_mean, by = c("age", "sex")) |> 
         mutate("centered" = height - mu)) +
  geom_line(aes(x = age, y = centered, color = sex, group = subject),
            alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.75) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#1e3a5f", "#e63946")) +
  labs(title = "Functional mean of height trajectories AFTER CENTERED",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Deviation from the functional mean") +
  theme_fda()
gg1 / gg2
```


:::
:::

---

## The Functional Variance $\sigma^2(t)$

::: {.notes}

The variance peak around age 11–13 reflects heterogeneity in the timing of the pubertal growth spurt — children differ most from each other at those ages.

*A parametric longitudinal model cannot reveal this for two reasons. First, the mean shape is fixed in advance: a quadratic has exactly one turning point and cannot capture the sharp acceleration-deceleration of the growth spurt. Second, the variance is also parametrized: a standard mixed model assumes constant sigma
or AR(1) correlation — it cannot detect that variability is higher at t≈12t 
t≈12 than at t=5t = 5
t=5, because that peak comes from timing heterogeneity, not from a parameter the model ever asks about.*

*A parametric model answers the question you ask of it. "What is β2\beta_2
β2?" — it will answer. But "at which ages are children most different from each other?" requires estimating σ2(t)\sigma^2(t)
σ2(t) freely as a function — and only FDA does that.*

:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
We can also define the **variance function**:

$$\sigma^2(t) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[x_i(t) - \mu(t)\right]^2$$

This tells us: *at each age $t$, how much do children differ from the average?*



:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r fig-variance}
#| fig-height: 9
var_t <- apply(girls, 1, var)

p1 <- ggplot(tb_curves |> filter(sex == "female"), aes(age, height, group = subject)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.18, color = "#1e3a5f", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = tb_mean |> filter(sex == "female"),
            aes(age, mu, group = 1),
            color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Individual curves + mean (females)",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_fda()

p2 <- ggplot(tibble(age = ages, v = var_t), aes(age, v)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#e63946", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = 12, xend = 12,
           y = 0, yend = max(var_t)*0.95,
           linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 12.2, y = max(var_t)*0.65,
           label = "Peak: pubertal timing", size = 4,
           hjust = 0, color = "grey30") +
  labs(title = expression(sigma^2*(t)*": variance function"),
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Variance") +
  theme_fda()

p1 / p2 + plot_layout(heights = c(1.5, 1))
```
:::
:::

---

## The functional covariance $C(s, t)$

::: {.notes}

The diagonal is \sigma^2(t)
σ2(t) — variance at each age. The brightest point around s=t≈11s = t \approx 11
s=t≈11–1212
12 confirms that girls differ most from each other during the pubertal growth spurt.

Off-diagonal: bottom-left corner is dark (early ages, low variance — all children similar at age 2–3); central-upper zone is bright (high covariance between intermediate and late ages — tall at 10 tends to mean tall at 15); early vs late ages are intermediate (being tall at 3 predicts adult height only weakly).

* Sex differences: boys' diagonal peak reaches ~80 vs ~50 in girls — more absolute variability. The peak is shifted to s=t≈13s = t \approx 13
s=t≈13–1515
15 in boys, consistent with a later and more prolonged pubertal spurt. The off-diagonal high-covariance region is also broader in boys, suggesting greater heterogeneity in pubertal timing. Both sexes show a dark bottom-left corner (s,t<5s, t < 5
s,t<5), but in boys it extends further — individual differences take longer to emerge.


:::
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
**Multi covariance:** a $p \times p$ matrix $\Sigma_{jk} = \text{Cov}(X_j, X_k)$

**Functional covariance:** a **surface** over $T \times T$

$$C(s,t) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n [x_i(s)-\mu(s)][x_i(t)-\mu(t)]$$

<br>

::: {.fragment}

::: {style="font-size: 93%;"}

- $C(t,t) = \sigma^2(t)$ — variance function on diagonal
- Off-diagonal: how much does height at age $s$ co-vary with height at age $t$?
- Decays away from diagonal → short memory
- Stays high everywhere → smooth, persistent process

:::
:::

:::

::: {.column width="53%"}

```{r fig-cov-surface}
#| fig-height: 10.7
cov_mat <- cov(t(girls))   # p × p covariance matrix

cov_df <- expand.grid(s = ages, t = ages) |>
  mutate(C = as.vector(cov_mat))

gg1 <-
  ggplot(cov_df, aes(s, t, fill = C)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "C(s,t)") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Functional covariance surface C(s, t)",
       subtitle = "Berkeley Growth Study — 54 girls",
       x = "Age s (years)", y = "Age t (years)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

cov_mat <- cov(t(boys))

cov_df <- expand.grid(s = ages, t = ages) |>
  mutate(C = as.vector(cov_mat))

gg2 <-
  ggplot(cov_df, aes(s, t, fill = C)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "C(s,t)") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(subtitle = "Berkeley Growth Study — 39 boys",
       x = "Age s (years)", y = "Age t (years)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "right", 
        plot.title = element_blank()) 
gg1 / gg2
```
:::
:::


---

## Why $C(s,t)$ is not just a big matrix?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}

::: {style="font-size: 92%;"}
**The multivariate cov matrix depends on measurement design.**

* Study A measures at ages: 2, 5, 8, 12, 16  
* Study B measures at ages: 3, 6, 10, 14

$\Sigma_A$ and $\Sigma_B$ are **not comparable** — different indices and sizes.

<br>

::: {.fragment}

**The functional covariance $C(s,t)$ is a property of the process**, not of the design. It can be evaluated at *any* pair of ages $(s, t)$, regardless of when measurements were taken.

→ Enables **harmonization** across studies with different measurement schedules.  
→ Enables **prediction** at unobserved time points.  

:::

:::
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

```{r fig-cov-slices}
#| fig-height: 13.5

# Covariance slices: C(s, ·) for a few fixed values of s
slice_ages <- c(2, 8, 12, 17)
idx        <- sapply(slice_ages, function(a) which.min(abs(ages - a)))

slice_df <- map_dfr(seq_along(slice_ages), function(k) {
  tibble(
    t     = ages,
    C     = cov_mat[idx[k], ],
    fixed = paste0("s = ", slice_ages[k], " yrs")
  )
}) |> 
  mutate("fixed" =
           factor(fixed, levels = c("s = 2 yrs", "s = 8 yrs",
                                    "s = 12 yrs", "s = 17 yrs")))

ggplot(slice_df, aes(t, C, color = fixed)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1", name = "Fixed age s") +
  labs(title = "Covariance slices C(s, ·) for fixed s",
       subtitle = "How much does height at age s co-vary with height at each age t?",
       x = "Age t (years)", y = "C(s, t)") +
  theme_fda()
```
:::
:::



# From observations to population {background-color="#1e3a5f"}

Functional bases

---


## From observations to population: basis

Data arrive as discrete, noisy measurements:

$$\{(t_{ij},\, y_{ij})\}_{j=1}^{m_i}, \quad y_{ij} = x_i(t_{ij}) + \varepsilon_{ij}$$

where $m_i\quad$ represents the number of timepoints for subject $j$ and $t_{ij}$ the time point in which $j$-th measures was collected for $i$-th subject.

::: {.fragment}

**Goal:** recover the underlying function $x_i(t)$.

:::

::: {.fragment}

### Strategy — basis representation

::: {style="font-size: 90%;"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}

$$\widehat{x}_i(t) =  \sum_{k=1}^{K} c_{ik}\, \phi_k(t)$$

- $\phi_k(t)$: known basis functions (B-splines, Fourier, wavelets...)
- $c_{ik}$: subject-specific coefficients, estimated from data

:::

::: {.column width="35%"}

Once $\widehat{x}_i(t)$ is available, we can: 

✅ Evaluate at any $t$  
✅ Differentiate (velocity, acceleration)  
✅ Integrate  
✅ Feed into functional models

:::
:::
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
We observe discrete noisy snapshots of a continuous curve — the goal is to recover the underlying function. Basis expansion is the standard strategy: express each curve as a weighted sum of K known basis functions, then estimate the subject-specific coefficients by minimizing a penalized least squares criterion. Once the smooth function is available, we can do things impossible with discrete measurements: evaluate at any unobserved time point, differentiate to get velocity and acceleration, integrate, and feed the estimated function directly into functional regression or FPCA. The choice of basis (B-splines, Fourier, wavelets) depends on the nature of the process — periodic, non-periodic, or with localized transient features.

:::
---


## From observations to population: basis



### Strategy — basis representation

$$\widehat{x}_i(t) =  \sum_{k=1}^{K} c_{ik}\, \phi_k(t)$$

- $\phi_k(t)$: known basis functions (B-splines, Fourier, wavelets...)
- $c_{ik}$: subject-specific coefficients, estimated from data


<br>

::: {.fragment}

Two main families of bases exist in FDA:

* **Fixed bases**: the functions $\phi_k(t)$ are chosen **BEFORE** seeing the data — their shape is determined by construction (B-splines, Fourier, wavelets). Subject-specific coefficients $c_{ik}$ are then estimated by minimizing a data fit criterion.

* **Data-driven bases**: the functions $\phi_k(t)$ are estimated from the **data themselves** — specifically from the **sample covariance structure**. They have no closed-form expression prior to estimation, and change with every new sample. The canonical example is FPCA, where the basis functions are the eigenfunctions of the estimated covariance operator.

:::



---




## Fixed bases

::: {.notes}

Based on polynomials of degree d

Imaging divide the time axis into intervals at fixed points called knots. On each interval you fit a polynomial, and you force them to join smoothly at the knots. Each basis function is just one of those local polynomial pieces.


<br>

Based on Sines and cosines at increasing frequencies — each basis function oscillates over the entire domain.

<br>

Scaled and shifted copies of a single oscillating function — each basis function is localized in both time and frequency simultaneously.

Take a small wave that starts at zero, oscillates briefly, and returns to zero — a wavelet. Now make copies of it: some stretched (capturing slow variations), some compressed (capturing fast transients), placed at different positions along the time axis. Each copy sees only a small piece of the signal, at a specific resolution. Together they cover everything.

:::


::: {.notes}

Fourier — periodicidad global
La señal es periódica en todo el dominio y con una estructura de frecuencias estacionaria — las frecuencias presentes son las mismas en t=0t=0
t=0 que en t=20t=20
t=20. La base de Fourier asume que si hay una oscilación a frecuencia ω\omega
ω, esa oscilación existe en todas partes.

El gráfico de Fourier que ves es correcto en ese sentido — las curvas tienen un patrón que se repite a lo largo del día, y las frecuencias son globales.

Wavelets — localización temporal
La señal puede tener oscilaciones pero solo en ciertos momentos. Un spike de EEG a t=0.3t=0.3
t=0.3 no implica nada sobre lo que ocurre a t=0.7t=0.7
t=0.7. Las wavelets pueden decir exactamente eso: "hay energía a esta frecuencia, pero solo aquí".

El problema del gráfico que ves es que las curvas sintéticas que generé no ilustran bien esto — parecen periódicas globalmente. Lo que debería mostrar son curvas que son planas la mayor parte del tiempo con transientes locales abruptos en momentos concretos.

La frontera precisa es:

Fourier es óptimo cuando la estructura de frecuencias es estacionaria — igual en todo el dominio. Wavelets son óptimas cuando las frecuencias son no estacionarias — aparecen y desaparecen localmente.

Penalización en b-splines: \int_\mathcal{T} \left[x_i''(t)\right]^2 dt

ourier — penalización sobre la energía en frecuencias altas:
min⁡ci∑j=1mi[yij−∑kcikϕk(tij)]2+λ∑kωk2 cik2\min_{\mathbf{c}_i} \sum_{j=1}^{m_i} \left[y_{ij} - \sum_k c_{ik} \phi_k(t_{ij})\right]^2 + \lambda \sum_k \omega_k^2\, c_{ik}^2ci​min​j=1∑mi​​[yij​−k∑​cik​ϕk​(tij​)]2+λk∑​ωk2​cik2​
Donde ωk\omega_k
ωk​ es la frecuencia de la kk
k-ésima función base. Como ϕk′′(t)=−ωk2ϕk(t)\phi_k''(t) = -\omega_k^2 \phi_k(t)
ϕk′′​(t)=−ωk2​ϕk​(t), penalizar ∫[x′′]2\int [x'']^2
∫[x′′]2 equivale a penalizar los coeficientes de las frecuencias altas — la penalización es
diagonal en la base de Fourier, lo que hace el problema muy eficiente computacionalmente.

Wavelets — umbralización de coeficientes, no penalización de derivadas:
min⁡ci∑j=1mi[yij−∑j,kcijk ψjk(tij)]2+λ∑j,k∣cijk∣\min_{\mathbf{c}_i} \sum_{j=1}^{m_i} \left[y_{ij} - \sum_{j,k} c_{ijk}\, \psi_{jk}(t_{ij})\right]^2 + \lambda \sum_{j,k} |c_{ijk}|ci​min​j=1∑mi​​​yij​−j,k∑​cijk​ψjk​(tij​)​2+λj,k∑​∣cijk​∣
Donde ψjk(t)=2j/2ψ(2jt−k)\psi_{jk}(t) = 2^{j/2}\psi(2^j t - k)
ψjk​(t)=2j/2ψ(2jt−k) son las wavelets a escala jj
j y traslación kk
k. La penalización es una
norma L1L^1
L1 sobre los coeficientes
 — produce soluciones sparse, poniendo a cero los coeficientes pequeños. Es lo que se conoce como soft thresholding o LASSO funcional.
 
:::

```{r fig-wavelet-ex2}
#| fig-height: 6

#     0.3*sin(20*pi*t_eeg) + 0.6*(t_eeg > 0.5 & t_eeg < 0.65) + rnorm(200,0,0.05),

#        subtitle = "Localized transient features",
#        x = "Time (s)", y = "Signal") +
#   theme_fda() +
#   theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(size=11))
t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)

psi_haar <- function(t) {
  ifelse(t >= 0 & t < 0.5,  1,
  ifelse(t >= 0.5 & t < 1, -1, 0))
}

params <- list(
  list(j = 0, k = 0, label = "ψ(t) — mother"),
  list(j = 1, k = 0, label = "j=1, k=0"),
  list(j = 1, k = 1, label = "j=1, k=1"),
  list(j = 2, k = 1, label = "j=2, k=1"),
  list(j = 2, k = 2, label = "j=2, k=2")
)

df_wav_basis <- map_dfr(params, function(p) {
  tibble(
    t     = t,
    y     = 2^(p$j / 2) * psi_haar(2^p$j * t - p$k),
    label = p$label
  )
})

ggplot(df_wav_basis, aes(t, y, color = label)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo", name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title    = "Haar wavelet basis functions ψ_{j,k}(t)",
    subtitle = expression(psi[j*","*k](t) == 2^{j/2}~psi(2^j~t - k)),
    x = "t", y = expression(psi[j*","*k](t))
  ) +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}

**Use when:** local, transient features matter.  
*EEG spikes, accelerometry bursts, gene expression pulses.*

## Fixed bases



```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
library(fda)

t    <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 200)
ages <- growth$age

# ── Individuo: primera niña del Berkeley Growth Study
y_obs  <- growth$hgtf[, 1]
t_obs  <- ages

# ── 1. B-SPLINES ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
K_bs       <- 10
bs_basis   <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = range(t_obs), nbasis = K_bs, norder = 4)
bs_fdpar   <- fdPar(bs_basis, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-1)
bs_smooth  <- smooth.basis(t_obs, y_obs, bs_fdpar)
bs_fitted  <- eval.fd(t_obs, bs_smooth$fd)

df_bs <- bind_rows(
  tibble(t = t_obs, y = y_obs,              type = "Observed"),
  tibble(t = t_obs, y = as.numeric(bs_fitted), type = "B-spline fit")
)

p_bs <- ggplot(df_bs |> filter(type == "Observed"),
               aes(t, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, color = "grey50", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = df_bs |> filter(type == "B-spline fit"),
            aes(t, y), color = "#2a9d8f", linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(title = "B-splines",
       subtitle = expression(hat(x)(t) == sum(c[k]*B[k](t), k=1, K)),
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_fda()

# ── 2. FOURIER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Fourier funciona mejor con datos periódicos — usamos señal circadiana simulada
set.seed(7)
t_fourier  <- seq(0, 24, length.out = 100)
y_fourier  <- 2 + sin(2*pi*t_fourier/24) +
              0.4*sin(4*pi*t_fourier/24) +
              0.2*cos(6*pi*t_fourier/24) +
              rnorm(100, 0, 0.12)

fou_basis  <- create.fourier.basis(rangeval = c(0, 24), nbasis = 9)
fou_fdpar  <- fdPar(fou_basis, lambda = 1e-4)
fou_smooth <- smooth.basis(t_fourier, y_fourier, fou_fdpar)
fou_fitted <- eval.fd(t_fourier, fou_smooth$fd)

df_fou <- bind_rows(
  tibble(t = t_fourier, y = y_fourier,              type = "Observed"),
  tibble(t = t_fourier, y = as.numeric(fou_fitted), type = "Fourier fit")
)

p_fou <- ggplot(df_fou |> filter(type == "Observed"), aes(t, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, color = "grey50", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = df_fou |> filter(type == "Fourier fit"),
            aes(t, y), color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(title = "Fourier",
       subtitle = expression(hat(x)(t) == sum(c[k]*phi[k](t), k=1, K)),
       x = "Hour of day", y = "Activity") +
  theme_fda()

# ── 3. WAVELETS ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Señal con transientes locales — reconstrucción por umbralización
library(wavethresh)

# Señal con bursts locales
set.seed(42)
n      <- 256   # wavethresh necesita potencia de 2
t_wav  <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n)
y_wav  <- 0.05 * rnorm(n) +
          1.2  * exp(-((t_wav - 0.20)^2) / (2*0.03^2)) * sin(2*pi*18*t_wav) +
          1.0  * exp(-((t_wav - 0.65)^2) / (2*0.04^2)) * sin(2*pi*10*t_wav)

# Descomposición wavelet + umbralización suave
wt        <- wd(y_wav, filter.number = 4, family = "DaubExPhase")
wt_thresh <- threshold(wt, policy = "universal", type = "soft")
y_recon   <- wr(wt_thresh)

df_wav2 <- bind_rows(
  tibble(t = t_wav, y = y_wav,    type = "Observed"),
  tibble(t = t_wav, y = y_recon,  type = "Wavelet fit")
)

p_wav <- ggplot(df_wav2 |> filter(type == "Observed"), aes(t, y)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = df_wav2 |> filter(type == "Wavelet fit"),
            aes(t, y), color = "#e9c46a", linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(title = "Wavelets",
       subtitle = expression(hat(x)(t) == sum(c[jk]*psi[jk](t), j,k)),
       x = "Time (s)", y = "Signal") +
  theme_fda()

# ── Combinar ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(p_bs | p_fou | p_wav) +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Representing data in each basis",
    subtitle = "Points/line: observed data — colored line: basis reconstruction",
    theme    = theme(
      plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15, color = "#0f1f3d"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "grey40")
    )
  )
```

## Fixed bases

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}

$$\min_{\mathbf{c}_i} \; \sum_{j=1}^{m_i} \left[y_{ij} - \sum_k c_{ik}\phi_k(t_{ij})\right]^2 + \; \lambda *Penalty(ci)$$

:::



```{r}
#| fig-height: 4

# Use subject 1 (girl), add noise to simulate realistic observations
set.seed(42)
subject1 <- girls[, 1]
noisy_obs <- subject1 + rnorm(length(ages), 0, 2.5)

lambdas    <- c(1e-4, 1e0, 1e4)
lambda_lab <- c("λ very small\n(interpolation)", "λ moderate\n(good fit)", "λ very large\n(over-smoothed)")
colors     <- c("#e63946", "#2a9d8f", "#e9c46a")

# Fit three smooths
fitted_list <- lapply(lambdas, function(lam) {
  fdPar_obj  <- fdPar(spline_basis, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = lam)
  sm         <- smooth.basis(ages, noisy_obs, fdPar_obj)
  fitted_vals <- eval.fd(ages, sm$fd)
  tibble(age = ages, fitted = as.numeric(fitted_vals))
})

obs_df <- tibble(age = ages, y = noisy_obs)

plots <- lapply(seq_along(lambdas), function(k) {
  ggplot(obs_df, aes(age, y)) +
    geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7, color = "grey40") +
    geom_line(data = fitted_list[[k]],
              aes(age, fitted), color = colors[k], linewidth = 1.4) +
    labs(title = lambda_lab[k], x = "Age", y = "Height") +
    theme_fda() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12, color = colors[k]))
})

(plots[[1]] | plots[[2]] | plots[[3]])
```


::: {.notes}

$\lambda$ is typically selected by **GCV** (generalized cross-validation) or leave-one-out CV, balancing fit quality against smoothness.

:::

---

## FPCA

> Fixed bases are chosen by the analyst. FPCA lets the data choose


::: {style="font-size: 87%;"}

**Classical PCA** — find the unit vector $\mathbf{v}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^p$ 
maximizing the variance of scalar projections:

$$\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_1 = \underset{\|\mathbf{v}\|=1}{\arg\max} \; \text{Var}\left(\mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{v}\right) = \underset{\|\mathbf{v}\|=1}{\arg\max} \; \text{Var}\left(\sum_{j=1}^p x_{ij} v_j\right) = \underset{\|\mathbf{v}\|=1}{\arg\max} \; \text{Var}\left( \langle \mathbf{x}_i^\top ,\mathbf{v} \rangle_{\mathbb{R}^p}\right)$$

::: {.fragment}

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Projection = inner product

$\mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{v}$ is the **inner product in $\mathbb{R}^p$**: the projection of the individual $i$ into the Principal Component $\mathbf{v}$

:::

:::

::: {.fragment}

**FPCA** — find the unit function $\phi_1(t) \in L^2(T)~$ maximizing the variance of functional projections:

$$\widehat{\phi}_1 = \underset{\|\phi\|=1}{\arg\max} \; \text{Var}\left(\langle x_i, \phi \rangle\right) = \underset{\|\phi\|=1}{\arg\max} \; \text{Var}\left(\int_T x_i(t) \,\phi(t)\,dt\right)$$

:::

::: {.fragment}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The only thing that changes
The inner product — from a **finite sum** to an **integral**. The rest is structurally identical: just replacing  projection the inner product by $\langle x_i, \phi \rangle_{L^2} = \int_T x_i(t) \,\phi(t)\,dt$


:::

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The analogy with classical PCA is exact and worth dwelling on. In PCA, 
we project each observation onto a direction in R^p — a vector — and 
maximize the variance of those scalar projections. The projection is a 
dot product: a sum over p coordinates.

In FPCA we do the same thing, but our observations are functions and our 
components are functions. The projection is now an integral — the L2 inner 
product. The score xi_{ik} tells you how much of component phi_k is present 
in subject i's curve, exactly as a PCA score tells you how much of 
eigenvector v_k is present in subject i's vector.

The solution is also structurally identical: in PCA you solve the 
eigenproblem for the covariance matrix Sigma. In FPCA you solve the 
eigenproblem for the covariance operator C — which is an integral operator 
instead of a matrix, but the math is the same.
:::



::: {.notes}

Hemos visto que podemos representar cualquier curva en una base fija — B-splines, Fourier, wavelets. Pero estas bases tienen un problema: las elegimos nosotros, antes de ver los datos, basándonos en supuestos sobre el proceso. No hay ninguna garantía de que sean eficientes para describir la variabilidad que realmente existe en nuestra muestra.

La pregunta natural es: ¿existe una base óptima — una que capture la máxima variabilidad de los datos con el mínimo número de componentes?

La respuesta es sí, y se llama FPCA.
:::

---

## The Karhunen-Loève Theorem

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}

Any square-integrable centered stochastic process $X(t)$ admits the decomposition:

$$x_i(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \xi_{ik}\, \phi_k(t) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{K} \xi_{ik}\, \phi_k(t)$$

- $\phi_k(t)$ — **orthonormal eigenFUNCTIONS** of $C(s, t)$.
- $\xi_{ik} = \langle x_i , \phi_k \rangle = \int x_i(t) \phi_k(t) dt \quad$ **scores** of subject $i$ on component $k$
- $\text{Cov}(\xi_{ik}, \xi_{il}) = \lambda_k\, \mathbf{1}_{k=l}\quad$: scores are **uncorrelated**
- $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \ldots \geq 0\quad$ **eigenvalues**, ordered by variance explained




:::

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{r fig-scree}
#| fig-height: 5
data("growth")
ages  <- growth$age
girls <- growth$hgtf

bs_basis <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = range(ages),
                                  nbasis = 15, norder = 4)
bs_fdpar <- fdPar(bs_basis, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-1)
girls_fd <- smooth.basis(ages, girls, bs_fdpar)$fd
fpca_res <- pca.fd(girls_fd, nharm = 4)
pve      <- round(fpca_res$varprop * 100, 1)

scree_df <- tibble(
  k   = 1:4,
  pve = pve,
  cum = cumsum(pve)
)

ggplot(scree_df, aes(k, pve)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.85, width = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cum), color = "#e63946",
            linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(y = cum), color = "#e63946", size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(y = pve, label = paste0(pve, "%")),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 3.8,
            color = "#0f1f3d", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name     = "Variance explained (%)",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~., name = "Cumulative (%)")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:4,
                     labels = paste0("PC", 1:4)) +
  labs(title    = "Scree plot — Berkeley Growth Study",
       subtitle = "Bars: per component    Dashed: cumulative",
       x = NULL) +
  theme_fda()
```

:::
:::

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## Three key consequences

**1. Optimality** — no other basis of $K$ functions captures more total variance. Functional analogue of the Eckart-Young theorem.

**2. Dimensionality reduction** — each subject is represented by $(\xi_{i1}, \ldots, \xi_{iK}) \in \mathbb{R}^K$. A function compressed into $K$ numbers.

**3. Variance explained** — $\lambda_k / \sum_j \lambda_j$, exactly as in classical PCA.
:::

:::


::: {.notes}
The Karhunen-Loève theorem is the theoretical backbone of FPCA. 
The decomposition always exists for any square-integrable process — 
it is not an approximation, it is exact in the limit of infinitely 
many components.

The three consequences are worth emphasizing separately.

First, optimality: the eigenfunctions are the best possible basis 
for this particular dataset. Any other K functions — B-splines, 
Fourier, anything — will explain less variance with K components. 
This is the functional version of the Eckart-Young theorem, which 
says that the SVD gives the best low-rank approximation of a matrix.

Second, dimensionality reduction: this is what makes FPCA practically 
useful. We started with functions — infinite-dimensional objects. 
We end up with a vector of K numbers per subject. Those numbers can 
be fed into any standard multivariate method: clustering, regression, 
classification, survival analysis.

Third, variance explained: the interpretation is identical to classical 
PCA. The scree plot on the right shows that in the Berkeley Growth Study, 
the first component alone explains the vast majority of variance — 
most of the between-girl variability is simply about overall height level.
:::


::: {.notes}
The Karhunen-Loève theorem guarantees that the decomposition exists and 
is optimal. The key message is that each subject i is now represented by 
a vector of K scores — a finite-dimensional summary of an infinite-dimensional 
object. Those scores inherit the geometry of L2: they are uncorrelated, 
and the variance of the k-th score is exactly the k-th eigenvalue.

The scree plot shows how many components are needed. In the Berkeley Growth 
Study, the first component alone explains most of the variance — height 
trajectories are mostly determined by overall size, with subsequent 
components capturing progressively subtler features like growth timing.
:::
