## FPCA


```{r fig-fpca-full}
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "FPCA-based reconstruction"
mu_t  <- eval.fd(ages, mean.fd(girls_fd))
efuns <- eval.fd(ages, fpca_res$harmonics)
pve   <- round(fpca_res$varprop * 100, 1)

# Panel 1: eigenfunctions
ef_df <- as.data.frame(efuns[, 1:3]) |>
  setNames(paste0("PC", 1:3, " (", pve[1:3], "%)")) |>
  mutate(age = ages) |>
  pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "component", values_to = "value")

p1 <- ggplot(ef_df, aes(age, value, color = component)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("#e63946", "#2a9d8f", "#457b9d"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Eigenfunctions",
    subtitle = "Each captures a mode of variation",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = expression(phi[k](t))
  ) +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# Panel 2: score plot
scores_df <- as.data.frame(fpca_res$scores[, 1:3]) |>
  setNames(paste0("PC", 1:3)) |>
  mutate(subject = 1:54)

idx_high <- which.max(scores_df$PC1)
idx_low  <- which.min(scores_df$PC1)

p2 <- ggplot(scores_df, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = scores_df[idx_high, ],
             aes(PC1, PC2), size = 4, color = "#e63946") +
  geom_point(data = scores_df[idx_low, ],
             aes(PC1, PC2), size = 4, color = "#2a9d8f") +
  annotate("text",
           x = scores_df$PC1[idx_high] - 0.5,
           y = scores_df$PC2[idx_high] - 3,
           label = "Tall", color = "#e63946",
           fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text",
           x = scores_df$PC1[idx_low] + 12,
           y = scores_df$PC2[idx_low] - 3,
           label = "Short", color = "#2a9d8f",
           fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, hjust = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Score plot: PC1 vs PC2",
    x = paste0("Score 1 (", pve[1], "% var)"),
    y = paste0("Score 2 (", pve[2], "% var)")
  ) +
  theme_fda()

# Panel 3: reconstruction
recon <- function(idx, npc = 3) {
  as.numeric(mu_t) +
    rowSums(sapply(1:npc, function(k)
      fpca_res$scores[idx, k] * efuns[, k]))
}

recon_df <- bind_rows(
  tibble(age = ages, y = as.numeric(mu_t), type = "Mean"),
  tibble(age = ages, y = recon(idx_high),  type = "High PC1 score"),
  tibble(age = ages, y = recon(idx_low),   type = "Low PC1 score")
)

p3 <- ggplot(recon_df, aes(age, y, color = type, linewidth = type)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Mean"           = "#0f1f3d",
      "High PC1 score" = "#e63946",
      "Low PC1 score"  = "#2a9d8f"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(
    values = c(
      "Mean"           = 1.5,
      "High PC1 score" = 1.2,
      "Low PC1 score"  = 1.2
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Reconstruction (3 PC)",
    subtitle = expression(
      hat(x)[i](t) == mu(t) + xi[i1]*phi[1](t) + xi[i2]*phi[2](t)
    ),
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Height (cm)"
  ) +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

idx_high <- which.max(scores_df$PC2)
idx_low  <- which.min(scores_df$PC2)

recon_df <- bind_rows(
  tibble(age = ages, y = as.numeric(mu_t), type = "Mean"),
  tibble(age = ages, y = recon(idx_high),  type = "High PC2 score"),
  tibble(age = ages, y = recon(idx_low),   type = "Low PC2 score")
)

p4 <- ggplot(recon_df, aes(age, y, color = type, linewidth = type)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Mean"           = "#0f1f3d",
      "High PC2 score" = "#e63946",
      "Low PC2 score"  = "#2a9d8f"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(
    values = c(
      "Mean"           = 1.5,
      "High PC2 score" = 1.2,
      "Low PC2 score"  = 1.2
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  guides(color = "none", linewidth = "none") +
  labs(
    # title    = "Reconstruction (2 PC)",
    # subtitle = expression(
    #   hat(x)[i](t) == mu(t) + xi[i1]*phi[1](t) + xi[i2]*phi[2](t)
    # ),
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Height (cm)"
  ) +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(plot.title = element_blank(),
        plot.subtitle = element_blank())

# Combine
(p1 | p2 | p3) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(2, 3, 3)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "FPCA in practice - Berkeley Growth Study",
    theme = theme_fda())
```

::: {.notes}
The three panels tell a complete story.

Panel 1 — the eigenfunctions. The first eigenfunction is roughly flat and 
positive — it captures overall height level. A girl with a high score on 
PC1 is simply taller than average at all ages. The second eigenfunction 
changes sign around age 12-13 — it captures the contrast between girls 
who grow fast early vs those who grow more in adolescence. The third 
captures finer variation around the pubertal growth spurt.

Panel 2 — the score plot. Each girl is now a point in R^K. The 
horizontal axis separates tall from short girls. The vertical axis 
separates early growers from late growers. This is the dimensionality 
reduction — from a function to two numbers, with interpretable meaning.

Panel 3 — reconstruction. The red and green curves are reconstructed 
from just two components plus the mean. The approximation is already 
very close to the observed trajectories, which confirms that two 
components capture most of the clinically relevant variability.

:::

---

## FPCA

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {style="font-size: 90%;"}

The eigenfunction problem to solve:

$$\int_T C(s,t)\, \phi_k(s)\, ds = \lambda_k\, \phi_k(t)$$

The functional analogue of $\Sigma \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}\quad$ in classical PCA.

<br>

::: {.fragment}

**Step 1** — Estimate

$$\widehat{C}(s,t) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[\widehat{x}_i(s) - \widehat{\mu}(s)\right]\left[\widehat{x}_i(t) - \widehat{\mu}(t)\right]$$

from the $n$ smoothed curves.

:::

::: {.fragment}

**Step 2 — Discretize** the integral equation:
$\widehat{\mathbf{C}}\, \boldsymbol{\phi}\, \Delta t = \lambda\, \boldsymbol{\phi}$

:::

::: {.fragment}

**Step 3 — Spectral decomposition** of $\widehat{\mathbf{C}}$:
$\widehat{\mathbf{C}} = \mathbf{V}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^\top$

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The key message here is that computing eigenfunctions is not magic —
it is a standard matrix eigendecomposition applied to the discretized
covariance surface. The functional setting adds one step at the beginning
(smoothing + covariance estimation) and one at the end (interpreting
eigenvectors as functions), but the core linear algebra is identical
to classical PCA.

In R, pca.fd() handles all three steps internally. The only decisions
you make are how many basis functions to use for smoothing, and how
many components to retain.

:::


:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}

| | Classical PCA | FPCA |
|--|--------------|------|
| Object | $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$ | $x_i(t) \in L^2(T)$ |
| Component | $\mathbf{v}_k \in \mathbb{R}^p$ | $\phi_k(t) \in L^2(T)$ |
| Inner product | $\sum_j x_{ij} v_j$ | $\int x_i(t)\phi_k(t)\,dt$ |
| Score | $\xi_{ik} = \mathbf{x}_i^\top \mathbf{v}_k$ | $\xi_{ik} = \langle x_i, \phi_k \rangle_{L^2}$ |
| Principal Component | eigenvector of $\Sigma$ | eigenfunction of $C(s,t)$ |
| # components | at most $p$ | countably infinite |

:::

:::

:::

---


## Derivatives as data: beyond mean/covariance

> Sometimes the signal is not in the curve itself — but in its rate of change.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}

::: {style="font-size: 72%;"}

Once $x_i(t)$ is represented in a basis, derivatives are
**free**

$$x_i'(t) = \frac{d}{dt}\sum_k c_{ik}\phi_k(t) = \sum_k c_{ik}\phi_k'(t)$$

This means you can treat **velocity** and **acceleration** as
functional observations — with their own mean and covariance.

**When are derivatives more informative?**

- The raw curve is dominated by a global trend that masks local features
- The scientific question is about **rates of change**, not levels
- The curve is very smooth and the interesting signal is in its curvature

:::

:::

::: {.column width="67%"}

```{r fig-derivatives}
#| fig-height: 6.6

library(fda)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(fda.usc)
data("tecator")
# tecator: 215 meat samples
# absorp: 215 x 100 matrix of NIR absorbance curves
# endpoints: wavelengths 850-1050 nm

wavelengths <- seq(850, 1050, length.out = 100)
absorp      <- tecator$absorp

# Smooth with B-splines
bs_basis <- create.bspline.basis(
  rangeval = range(wavelengths),
  nbasis   = 40,
  norder   = 6   # order 6 -> smooth enough for 2nd derivative
)
bs_fdpar <- fdPar(bs_basis, Lfdobj = 4, lambda = 1e-4)
absorp_fd <- smooth.basis(wavelengths, t(absorp$data), bs_fdpar)$fd

# Evaluate: curve, 1st and 2nd derivative
x0 <- eval.fd(wavelengths, absorp_fd, Lfd = 0)
x1 <- eval.fd(wavelengths, absorp_fd, Lfd = 1)
x2 <- eval.fd(wavelengths, absorp_fd, Lfd = 2)

# Select a subsample for visibility
idx <- sample(1:215, 40)

make_df <- function(mat, idx, varname) {
  as.data.frame(mat[, idx]) |>
    setNames(paste0("s", idx)) |>
    mutate(wavelength = wavelengths) |>
    pivot_longer(-wavelength,
                 names_to = "subject",
                 values_to = varname)
}

df0 <- make_df(x0, idx, "y")
df1 <- make_df(x1, idx, "y")
df2 <- make_df(x2, idx, "y")

# Fat content for coloring
fat <- tecator$y[, 1]   # % fat

color_df <- tibble(
  subject = paste0("s", idx),
  fat     = fat[idx]
)

add_fat <- function(df) left_join(df, color_df, by = "subject")

p0 <- ggplot(add_fat(df0), aes(wavelength, y,
                                group = subject, color = fat)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Fat %") +
  labs(title    = "Raw absorbance  x(t)",
       subtitle = "Curves look similar",
       x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "Absorbance") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p1 <- ggplot(add_fat(df1), aes(wavelength, y,
                                group = subject, color = fat)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Fat %") +
  labs(title    = "First derivative  x'(t)",
       subtitle = "Rates of change begin to separate them",
       x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "x'(t)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p2 <- ggplot(add_fat(df2), aes(wavelength, y,
                                group = subject, color = fat)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Fat %",
                        guide = guide_colorbar(
                          barwidth  = 0.8,
                          barheight = 6
                        )) +
  labs(title    = "Second derivative  x''(t)",
       subtitle = "Peaks reveal wavelengths linked to fat",
       x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "x''(t)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

(p0 | p1 | p2) +
  plot_annotation(
    title    = "Tecator dataset: NIR spectrometry of meat samples",
    theme = theme_fda()
  )
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is one of the most practically useful features of FDA that has
no clean analogue in multivariate or longitudinal analysis.

In multivariate analysis, you observe x_{ij} at fixed time points.
You can compute finite differences as a proxy for derivatives, but
these are noisy and depend heavily on the spacing of observations.

In FDA, once you have a smooth basis representation, differentiation
is exact and analytic — you just differentiate the basis functions,
which have known closed-form derivatives. The result is a new
functional object that you can analyze exactly like the original curves.

The spectrometry example is particularly clean: the raw absorbance
curves all look similar and are hard to distinguish. The second
derivative reveals peaks at specific wavelengths that correspond
to chemical bonds — the features that actually predict fat content.
This is why NIR spectrometry data is almost always analyzed in
derivative form in chemometrics.
:::



---

## Functional ANOVA (FANOVA)

> Does the mean function differ across groups?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {style="font-size: 76%;"}

**Classical ANOVA** tests whether group means differ in $\mathbb{R}$:

$$H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \ldots = \mu_G$$

**Functional ANOVA** extends this to function spaces:

$$H_0: \mu_1(t) = \mu_2(t) = \ldots = \mu_G(t) \quad \forall t \in T$$

The null hypothesis is now that **entire curves** are equal — not just scalar means.

<br>

**Test statistics** are typically based on:

$$F(t) = \frac{\text{Between-group variance at } t}{\text{Within-group variance at } t}$$

$F(t)$ is itself a **function** — it tells you at which time points the groups differ most. **Inference** can be done via **permutation tests** — reshuffle group labels, recompute $F(t)$, build a null distribution for $\|F\|$ or $\max_t F(t)$.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r fig-fanova}
#| fig-height: 9.5

data("growth")
ages  <- growth$age
girls <- growth$hgtf
boys  <- growth$hgtm

bs_basis <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = range(ages),
                                  nbasis = 15, norder = 4)
bs_fdpar <- fdPar(bs_basis, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-1)
girls_fd <- smooth.basis(ages, girls, bs_fdpar)$fd
boys_fd  <- smooth.basis(ages, boys,  bs_fdpar)$fd

mu_girls <- eval.fd(ages, mean.fd(girls_fd))
mu_boys  <- eval.fd(ages, mean.fd(boys_fd))

# Pointwise F-statistic (simplified)
var_girls <- apply(eval.fd(ages, girls_fd), 1, var)
var_boys  <- apply(eval.fd(ages, boys_fd),  1, var)
n_g <- ncol(girls); n_b <- ncol(boys)

grand_mean <- (rowMeans(girls) * n_g + rowMeans(boys) * n_b) / (n_g + n_b)
SS_between <- n_g * (mu_girls - grand_mean)^2 + n_b * (mu_boys - grand_mean)^2
SS_within  <- (n_g - 1) * var_girls + (n_b - 1) * var_boys
F_t        <- (SS_between / 1) / (SS_within / (n_g + n_b - 2))

df_means <- bind_rows(
  tibble(age = ages, mu = as.numeric(mu_girls), group = "Girls (n=54)"),
  tibble(age = ages, mu = as.numeric(mu_boys),  group = "Boys (n=39)")
)

p1 <- ggplot(df_means, aes(age, mu, color = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#e63946", "#1e3a5f"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = expression("Group mean functions" ~ mu[g](t)),
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p2 <- ggplot(tibble(age = ages, F = as.numeric(F_t)), aes(age, F)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#e63946", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = qf(0.95, 1, n_g + n_b - 2),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 17, y = qf(0.95, 1, n_g + n_b - 2) + 5,
           label = "Critical value (95%)", color = "grey40", size = 5) +
  labs(title = "Pointwise F-statistic F(t)",
       subtitle = "Where do girls and boys differ most?",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "F(t)") +
  theme_fda()

p1 / p2 + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1))
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
FANOVA is the direct extension of ANOVA to functional data. The key
conceptual shift is that the null hypothesis is now a statement about
entire functions, not scalars.

The pointwise F-statistic F(t) is intuitive: at each age t, it measures
how much the group means differ relative to within-group variability.
High F(t) at age 13-15 tells you that boys and girls diverge most
during adolescence — which is exactly what the biology predicts.

Inference via permutation is the standard approach because the
distribution of functional test statistics is complex. You shuffle
the group labels many times, recompute the test statistic each time,
and use the empirical distribution as your null.

Key references: Ramsay & Silverman (2005)

If asked about multiple comparisons: the permutation test on a global
statistic (like the L2 norm of F(t)) naturally controls the familywise
error rate across the entire domain. Cuevas, Febrero & Fraiman
(2004), Computational Statistics & Data Analysis.

:::

---

## Functional Regression

> How does a functional predictor relate to an outcome?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {style="font-size: 82%;"}

Three main paradigms depending on the nature of predictor and response:

<br>

**Scalar-on-Function (SoF)**

$$Y_i = \alpha +  \langle x_i, \beta \rangle_{L^2} +\varepsilon_i = \alpha  + \int_T x_i(t)\,\beta(t)\,dt + \varepsilon_i$$

 The **coefficient function** $\beta(t)$ tells you which parts of the curve $x_i(t)$ matter most for predicting $Y_i$.

*Example: predict fat content (%) from NIR absorbance curve.*


:::

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r fig-regression-2}
#| fig-height: 7.5

library(fda)
library(fda.usc)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

# ── DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
data("tecator")
wavelengths <- seq(850, 1050, length.out = 100)
absorp      <- tecator$absorp$data   # 215 x 100
fat         <- tecator$y[, 1]        # % fat

data("growth")
ages  <- growth$age
girls <- growth$hgtf
boys  <- growth$hgtm

# ── 1. SCALAR-ON-FUNCTION ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Predict fat (scalar) from absorbance curve (function)
# via FPCA + linear regression on scores

bs_tec <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = range(wavelengths),
                                nbasis = 25, norder = 4)
fdpar_tec <- fdPar(bs_tec, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-3)
absorp_fd <- smooth.basis(wavelengths, t(absorp), fdpar_tec)$fd

fpca_tec  <- pca.fd(absorp_fd, nharm = 6)
scores_tec <- fpca_tec$scores

lm_sof    <- lm(fat ~ scores_tec)
fitted_sof <- fitted(lm_sof)

# Reconstruct beta(t) = sum_k beta_k * phi_k(t)
beta_coef <- coef(lm_sof)[-1]   # drop intercept
efuns_tec <- eval.fd(wavelengths, fpca_tec$harmonics)
beta_t    <- as.numeric(efuns_tec %*% beta_coef)

p_sof <- ggplot(tibble(wavelength = wavelengths, beta = beta_t),
                aes(wavelength, beta)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#e63946", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title    = "Scalar-on-Function",
    subtitle = expression(Y[i] == alpha + integral(x[i](t)*beta(t)*dt) + epsilon[i]),
    x = "Wavelength (nm)",
    y = expression(hat(beta)(t))
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 975, y = max(beta_t) * 0.8,
           label = "Predict fat %\nfrom absorbance curve",
           size = 5, color = "#e63946", fontface = "italic") +
  theme_fda()
p_sof
```

:::
:::

---

## Functional Regression

> How does a functional predictor relate to an outcome?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {style="font-size: 82%;"}

Three main paradigms depending on the nature of predictor and response:

<br>

**Function-on-Scalar (FoS)**

$$y_i(t) = \beta_0(t) + x_{i}\,\beta_1(t) + \varepsilon_i(t)$$

Response is a function, predictors are scalars. Each scalar predictor has a **functional coefficient** $\beta_j(t)$.

*Example: how does sex affect the entire growth curve?*

:::

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r fig-regression-3}
#| fig-height: 7.5

library(fda)
library(fda.usc)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

# ── DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
data("tecator")
wavelengths <- seq(850, 1050, length.out = 100)
absorp      <- tecator$absorp$data   # 215 x 100
fat         <- tecator$y[, 1]        # % fat

data("growth")
ages  <- growth$age
girls <- growth$hgtf
boys  <- growth$hgtm

# ── 1. SCALAR-ON-FUNCTION ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Predict fat (scalar) from absorbance curve (function)
# via FPCA + linear regression on scores

bs_tec <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = range(wavelengths),
                                nbasis = 25, norder = 4)
fdpar_tec <- fdPar(bs_tec, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-3)
absorp_fd <- smooth.basis(wavelengths, t(absorp), fdpar_tec)$fd

fpca_tec  <- pca.fd(absorp_fd, nharm = 6)
scores_tec <- fpca_tec$scores

lm_sof    <- lm(fat ~ scores_tec)
fitted_sof <- fitted(lm_sof)

# Reconstruct beta(t) = sum_k beta_k * phi_k(t)
beta_coef <- coef(lm_sof)[-1]   # drop intercept
efuns_tec <- eval.fd(wavelengths, fpca_tec$harmonics)
beta_t    <- as.numeric(efuns_tec %*% beta_coef)

p_sof <- ggplot(tibble(wavelength = wavelengths, beta = beta_t),
                aes(wavelength, beta)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#e63946", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title    = "Scalar-on-Function",
    subtitle = expression(Y[i] == alpha + integral(x[i](t)*beta(t)*dt) + epsilon[i]),
    x = "Wavelength (nm)",
    y = expression(hat(beta)(t))
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 950, y = max(beta_t) * 0.8,
           label = "Predict fat %\nfrom absorbance curve",
           size = 3.5, color = "#e63946", fontface = "italic") +
  theme_fda()

# ── 2. FUNCTION-ON-SCALAR ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Predict growth curve (function) from sex (scalar)
# beta_sex(t) = mean_boys(t) - mean_girls(t)

all_curves <- cbind(girls, boys)
sex_dummy  <- c(rep(0, 54), rep(1, 39))   # 0 = female, 1 = male

bs_gr <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = range(ages),
                               nbasis = 15, norder = 4)
fdpar_gr <- fdPar(bs_gr, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-1)
all_fd   <- smooth.basis(ages, all_curves, fdpar_gr)$fd

# Pointwise regression: x_i(t) = beta0(t) + beta1(t)*sex_i
mu_girls_t <- rowMeans(girls)
mu_boys_t  <- rowMeans(boys)
beta0_t    <- mu_girls_t                    # intercept = female mean
beta1_t    <- mu_boys_t - mu_girls_t       # sex effect = difference in means

df_fos <- bind_rows(
  tibble(age = ages, y = beta0_t,         label = "beta[0](t): female mean"),
  tibble(age = ages, y = beta0_t + beta1_t, label = "beta[0](t) + beta[1](t): male mean"),
  tibble(age = ages, y = beta1_t,          label = "beta[1](t): sex effect")
)

p_fos <- ggplot(df_fos |> filter(label != "beta[1](t): sex effect"),
                aes(age, y, color = label)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = tibble(age = ages,
                  ymin = mu_girls_t,
                  ymax = mu_boys_t),
    aes(age, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "#2a9d8f", alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("beta[0](t): female mean"             = "#e63946",
               "beta[0](t) + beta[1](t): male mean"  = "#1e3a5f"),
    labels = c(expression(beta[0](t)*": female mean"),
               expression(beta[0](t)+beta[1](t)*": male mean")),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Function-on-Scalar",
    subtitle = expression(x[i](t) == beta[0](t) + beta[1](t)*sex[i] + epsilon[i](t)),
    x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)"
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 14, y = 140,
           label = expression(beta[1](t)*": sex effect"),
           color = "#2a9d8f", size = 5.5, fontface = "italic") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 9))

# ── 3. FUNCTION-ON-FUNCTION ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Illustrate conceptually: beta(s,t) surface
# Reference: Garcia-Portugues, Alvarez-Liebana et al. (2021) SJOS

s_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 60)
t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 60)

beta_surf <- outer(s_grid, t_grid, function(s, t) {
  1.5 * exp(-3 * (s - 0.3)^2) * exp(-3 * (t - 0.4)^2) -
    exp(-3 * (s - 0.7)^2) * exp(-3 * (t - 0.7)^2)
})

surf_df <- expand.grid(s = s_grid, t = t_grid) |>
  mutate(beta = as.vector(beta_surf))

p_fof <- ggplot(surf_df, aes(s, t, fill = beta)) +
  geom_raster(interpolate = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2a9d8f", mid = "white", high = "#e63946",
    midpoint = 0, name = expression(beta(s,t))
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title    = "Function-on-Function",
    subtitle = expression(y[i](t) == integral(x[i](s)*beta(s,t)*ds) + epsilon[i](t)),
    x = "Domain of predictor (s)",
    y = "Domain of response (t)"
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.05,
           label = "Garcia-Portugues, Alvarez-Liebana\net al. (2021) SJOS",
           color = "grey30", size = 3, hjust = 0.5, fontface = "italic") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        legend.key.height = unit(0.8, "cm"))

# ── COMBINE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
p_fos
```

:::
:::

## Functional Regression

> How does a functional predictor relate to an outcome?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {style="font-size: 82%;"}

Three main paradigms depending on the nature of predictor and response:

<br>



**Function-on-Function (FoF)**

$$y_i(t) = \langle x_i, \beta(\cdot, t) \rangle_{L^2} =  \int_T x_i(s)\,\beta(s,t)\,ds + \varepsilon_i(t)$$

Both response and predictor are functions. The coefficient is a **surface** $\beta(s,t)$.

*Example: is there exists an increment in the global temperature respect to previous years?*


:::

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r fig-regression-fda}
#| fig-height: 8

library(goffda)
library(fda)
library(tidyverse)
data("aemet_temp")

with(aemet_temp, {
  ind_pred <- which((1974 <= df$year) & (df$year <= 1993))
  ind_resp <- which((1994 <= df$year) & (df$year <= 2013))
  aemet_pred <<- list("df" = df[ind_pred, ], "temp" = temp[ind_pred])
  aemet_resp <<- list("df" = df[ind_resp, ], "temp" = temp[ind_resp])
})

# ── Promediar por estacion dentro de cada periodo ────────────────────────────
mean_aemet <- function(x) {
  m <- tapply(
    X     = 1:nrow(x$temp$data),
    INDEX = x$df$ind,
    FUN   = function(i) colMeans(x$temp$data[i, , drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
  )
  x$temp$data <- do.call(rbind, m)
  return(x$temp)
}

X_fdata <- mean_aemet(aemet_pred)   # fdata: estaciones x 365
Y_fdata <- mean_aemet(aemet_resp)

X_mat   <- X_fdata$data
Y_mat   <- Y_fdata$data
t_dom   <- X_fdata$argvals

# Suavizar con base de Fourier (proceso periódico anual)
fou_basis <- create.fourier.basis(rangeval = range(t_dom), nbasis = 21)
fdpar_fou <- fdPar(fou_basis, lambda = 1e-2)

X_fd <- smooth.basis(t_dom, t(X_mat), fdpar_fou)$fd
Y_fd <- smooth.basis(t_dom, t(Y_mat), fdpar_fou)$fd

# FPCA del predictor
fpca_x  <- pca.fd(X_fd, nharm = 12)
scores_x <- fpca_x$scores         # n x K
efuns_x  <- eval.fd(t_dom, fpca_x$harmonics)  # 365 x K

# Regresion Y_fd ~ scores_x: para cada punto t del dominio de Y,
# regresion lineal de y_i(t) sobre los scores de x_i
Y_eval <- eval.fd(t_dom, Y_fd)    # 365 x n

# beta(s, t) = sum_k beta_k(t) * phi_k(s)
# Estimamos beta_k(t) para cada t por OLS
beta_mat <- solve(t(scores_x) %*% scores_x,
                  t(scores_x) %*% t(Y_eval))   # K x 365

# Reconstruir beta(s,t) = efuns_x %*% beta_mat
# efuns_x: 365 x K,  beta_mat: K x 365
# resultado: 365 x 365 (s x t)
beta_surf <- efuns_x %*% beta_mat

# Grid de meses para los ejes (usar medias mensuales para visualizar)
months_idx <- round(seq(1, 365, length.out = 13))
month_labs <- c("Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun",
                "Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec","Jan")

# Subsamplear la superficie a grid mensual para la visualizacion
s_idx <- round(seq(1, 365, length.out = 100))
t_idx <- round(seq(1, 365, length.out = 100))

surf_df <- expand.grid(
  s_idx = s_idx,
  t_idx = t_idx
) |>
  mutate(
    s    = t_dom[s_idx],
    t    = t_dom[t_idx],
    beta = mapply(function(si, ti) beta_surf[si, ti], s_idx, t_idx)
  )

# Limites simetricos
lim <- max(abs(quantile(surf_df$beta, c(0.02, 0.98))))

ggplot(surf_df, aes(s, t, fill = beta)) +
  geom_raster(interpolate = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low      = "#457b9d",
    mid      = "white",
    high     = "#e63946",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits   = c(-lim, lim),
    name     = expression(hat(beta)(s,t))
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = months_idx[-13],
    labels = month_labs[-13]
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = months_idx[-13],
    labels = month_labs[-13]
  ) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              color = "black", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept =  60,
              color = "black", linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = -60,
              color = "black", linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title    = "Function-on-Function: FPCR estimator",
    subtitle = expression(
      hat(beta)(s,t)*": AEMET temperature 1974-1993 "%->%"1994-2013"
    ),
    x = "Temperature in 1974-1993 (s)",
    y = "Temperature in 1994-2013 (t)",
    caption  = "Garcia-Portugues, Alvarez-Liebana et al. (2021). Scand. J. Stat., 48(2):502-528"
  ) +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Functional regression is one of the most practically useful tools in FDA
for health sciences. The three paradigms cover most real applications.

The coefficient function beta(t) in scalar-on-function regression has a
direct interpretation: wavelengths where beta(t) is large and positive
are wavelengths where high absorbance predicts high fat content. This is
directly interpretable in terms of the underlying chemistry (C-H bond
vibrations at specific wavelengths).

In the Tecator example, beta(t) is estimated via penalized regression
in a functional basis — implemented in the refund package via pfr().
The penalty controls smoothness of beta(t) exactly as in basis
smoothing.

Key packages: refund (Goldsmith et al.) for scalar-on-function and
function-on-scalar; FoFR for function-on-function.

Key references: Ramsay & Silverman (2005) Ch. 15; Goldsmith et al.
(2011), Biometrics; Reiss & Ogden (2007), JASA.

If asked about variable selection: there are functional LASSO extensions
that produce sparse beta(t) — equal to zero over entire intervals where
the predictor is irrelevant.
:::

---

## Functional Time Series

> What if the functions themselves are time correlated?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}

A **functional time series** is a sequence of functions:

$$x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_n(t)$$

where the **index** $i$ represents time (day, year, patient visit...) and each $x_i(t)$ is a curve over an intra-period domain $t$.

**Examples in health sciences:**

- Daily activity profiles observed over weeks: $x_{\text{day}}(\text{hour})$
- Yearly mortality curves by age: $x_{\text{year}}(\text{age})$
- Weekly EEG recordings: $x_{\text{week}}(\text{frequency})$

::: {.fragment}

**Key concepts:**

- **Functional autocorrelation**: $\text{Cov}(x_i(s), x_{i+h}(t))\quad$ — how does today's curve predict tomorrow's?
- **Forecasting**: predict $x_{n+1}(t)$ given $x_1(t), \ldots, x_n(t)$ — a whole curve forecast instead of scalar values.

:::

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r fig-fts}
#| fig-height: 9

set.seed(7)
n_days   <- 60
hours    <- seq(0, 24, length.out = 100)

# Simulate daily activity profiles with weekly seasonality + trend
sim_day <- function(day) {
  weekly_effect <- 0.3 * sin(2 * pi * day / 7)
  trend_effect  <- 0.005 * day
  base <- (1.5 + weekly_effect + trend_effect) *
          dnorm(hours, mean = 9 + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5), sd = 2) * 80 +
          dnorm(hours, mean = 17 + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5), sd = 1.5) * 50 +
          rnorm(length(hours), 0, 1)
  pmax(base, 0)
}

activity_mat <- sapply(1:n_days, sim_day)

# Show first 20 days colored by day index
sel_days <- c(1, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60)
act_df <- map_dfr(sel_days, function(d) {
  tibble(hour = hours, activity = activity_mat[, d], day = d)
})

p1 <- ggplot(act_df, aes(hour, activity, color = day, group = day)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Day", option = "magma") +
  labs(title    = "Daily activity profiles over 60 days",
       subtitle = "Each curve = one day. Color = time ordering.",
       x = "Hour of day", y = "Activity") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        legend.key.height = unit(0.8, "cm"))

# FPCA on the functional time series + scores as time series
bs_fts <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = range(hours), nbasis = 15, norder = 4)
fdpar_fts <- fdPar(bs_fts, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-2)
act_fd   <- smooth.basis(hours, activity_mat, fdpar_fts)$fd
fpca_fts <- pca.fd(act_fd, nharm = 2)

scores_ts <- tibble(
  day    = 1:n_days,
  score1 = fpca_fts$scores[, 1],
  score2 = fpca_fts$scores[, 2]
)

p2 <- ggplot(scores_ts, aes(day, score1)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2a9d8f", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE,
              color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title    = "PC1 score over time",
       subtitle = "Functional time series reduces to scalar time series on scores",
       x = "Day", y = "Score 1") +
  theme_fda()

# p1 / p2 + plot_layout(heights = c(1.2, 1))
p1
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Functional time series is a growing area at the intersection of FDA
and time series analysis. The key insight is that many health data
sources are naturally organized as sequences of curves — not just
one functional observation per subject, but a sequence of functional
observations where the ordering matters.

The FPCA + scalar time series approach is the most practical entry
point: decompose each daily curve into K scores, then apply standard
ARIMA, VAR, or state-space models to the score sequences. Forecasting
a future curve means forecasting future scores and reconstructing.

More advanced approaches model the functional autocorrelation directly
without going through FPCA first — see Bosq (2000) for the theoretical
foundations and Hyndman & Shang (2009) for a practical forecasting
approach used in mortality rate forecasting.

Key reference: Bosq (2000), Linear Processes in Function Spaces;
Hyndman & Shang (2009), Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics.
Package: ftsa in R.

If asked about COVID mortality data: daily age-specific mortality curves
by country form a functional time series — each day is a curve over age.
FDA revealed that different countries followed different functional
trajectories, not just different levels.
:::

---

## Functional Time Series

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}

The simplest and most studied model for functional time series
is the **Autoregressive Hilbertian process of order 1 — ARH(1)**:

$$X_n(t) = \Psi(X_{n-1})(t) + \varepsilon_n(t)$$

::: {.fragment}

- $\Psi$ is a **linear operator** — the functional
analogue of the AR(1) coefficient $\phi$, such that $\Psi(X_{n-1})(t) = \int_T \psi(s,t)\, X_{n-1}(s)\, ds$
- $\varepsilon_n(t)$ is a functional white noise — i.i.d. curves
with $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_n(t)] = 0\quad$ and $\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_n(s), \varepsilon_n(t)) = C_\varepsilon(s,t)$

:::

::: {.fragment}


**Stationarity condition:** $\|\Psi\|_{L^2} < 1$ — the operator
norm of $\Psi$ must be less than 1, analogous to $|\phi| < 1$ in scalar AR(1).

:::

:::

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r fig-arh1}
#| fig-height: 9

library(fda)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(42)

# ── Simular un proceso ARH(1) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Dominio
t_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 100)
n_obs  <- 80   # numero de curvas en la serie temporal

# Operador Psi representado por su kernel psi(s,t)
# Usamos un kernel suave y de norma < 1
psi_kernel <- function(s, t) {
  0.6 * exp(-3 * (s - t)^2)   # gaussiano: operacion local en tiempo
}
Psi_mat <- outer(t_grid, t_grid, psi_kernel) / length(t_grid)

# Innovaciones: curvas gaussianas suaves
sim_innovation <- function() {
  coefs <- rnorm(8, 0, 0.5)
  basis <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = c(0,1), nbasis = 8, norder = 4)
  as.numeric(eval.fd(t_grid, fd(matrix(coefs), basis)))
}

# Simular ARH(1): X_n = Psi(X_{n-1}) + eps_n
X_mat <- matrix(0, nrow = length(t_grid), ncol = n_obs)
X_mat[, 1] <- sim_innovation()
for (i in 2:n_obs) {
  X_mat[, i] <- Psi_mat %*% X_mat[, i-1] + sim_innovation()
}

# ── Panel 1: la serie temporal funcional ──────────────────────────────────────
sel <- c(1, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80)
ts_df <- map_dfr(sel, function(i) {
  tibble(t = t_grid, x = X_mat[, i], n = i)
})

p1 <- ggplot(ts_df, aes(t, x, color = n, group = n)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "n") +
  labs(
    title    = "ARH(1) — functional time series",
    subtitle = expression(X[n](t) == Psi(X[n-1])(t) + epsilon[n](t)),
    x = "t", y = expression(X[n](t))
  ) +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        legend.key.height = unit(0.6, "cm"))

# ── Panel 2: el kernel Psi(s,t) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
kern_df <- expand.grid(s = t_grid, t = t_grid) |>
  mutate(psi = as.vector(outer(t_grid, t_grid, psi_kernel)))

p2 <- ggplot(kern_df, aes(s, t, fill = psi)) +
  geom_raster(interpolate = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#457b9d", mid = "white", high = "#e63946",
    midpoint = 0, name = expression(psi(s,t))
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title    = "Autocorrelation kernel",
    subtitle = expression(Psi(X[n-1])(t) == integral(psi(s,t)*X[n-1](s)*ds)),
    x = "s  (previous curve)", y = "t  (next curve)"
  ) +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        legend.key.height = unit(0.8, "cm"))

# ── Panel 3: scores como serie temporal escalar ───────────────────────────────
bs_arh <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = c(0,1), nbasis = 12, norder = 4)
fdpar_arh <- fdPar(bs_arh, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-2)
X_fd   <- smooth.basis(t_grid, X_mat, fdpar_arh)$fd
fpca_arh <- pca.fd(X_fd, nharm = 3)
pve_arh  <- round(fpca_arh$varprop * 100, 1)

scores_arh <- as.data.frame(fpca_arh$scores[, 1:2]) |>
  setNames(c("PC1", "PC2")) |>
  mutate(n = 1:n_obs)

p3 <- ggplot(scores_arh, aes(n, PC1)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2a9d8f", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE,
              color = "#e63946", linewidth = 0.8,
              linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title    = "PC1 score as scalar time series",
    subtitle = paste0("PC1 explains ", pve_arh[1],
                      "% of variance — models as AR(1)"),
    x = "n (time index)", y = expression(xi[n*","*1])
  ) +
  theme_fda()

# ── Autocorrelacion de los scores ─────────────────────────────────────────────
acf_vals <- acf(scores_arh$PC1, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 15)
acf_df   <- tibble(
  lag = acf_vals$lag[-1],
  acf = acf_vals$acf[-1]
)
ci <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n_obs)

p4 <- ggplot(acf_df, aes(lag, acf)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(ci, -ci),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "#e63946", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4, color = "grey40") +
  labs(
    title    = "ACF of PC1 scores",
    subtitle = "Significant lag-1 autocorrelation confirms ARH(1) structure",
    x = "Lag", y = "ACF"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:15) +
  theme_fda()

# ── Combinar ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(p1 | p2) / (p3 | p4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Autoregressive Hilbertian process of order 1 — ARH(1)",
    theme = theme_fda()
  )
```

:::
:::

## Functional Depth Measures

> Which curves are central (median)? Which are outliers?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}

::: {style="font-size: 74%;"}

In $\mathbb{R}$, ordering observations is trivial. In **function spaces**, there is no natural ordering. But we can define **depth** — a measure of how **central** a curve is relative to the sample.


::: {.fragment}

A curve is deep if it is **surrounded by many other curves**. An outlier is a curve that lies in the periphery.

:::

::: {.fragment}

* **Fraiman-Muniz (FM) depth** — at each $t$, we measure how central $x_i(t)$ is relative to other curves, and then average.

:::

::: {.fragment}

* **Modified Band Depth (MBD)** *(Lopez-Pintado & Romo, 2009)*: a curve is deep if it spends most of its time inside the band formed by other curves (by any pair $(x_j, x_k)$)

$$D_{MBD}(x_i) = \binom{n}{2}^{-1}\sum_{j<k} \lambda\bigl(\{t: \min(x_j,x_k) \leq x_i \leq \max(x_j,x_k)\}\bigr)$$

:::

:::

:::

::: {.column width="52%"}

```{r fig-depth}
#| fig-height: 8

library(fda.usc)

data("growth")
ages  <- growth$age
girls <- growth$hgtf

# Compute MBD depth
fdata_girls <- fdata(t(girls), argvals = ages)
depth_mbd   <- depth.mode(fdata_girls)$dep

# Rank by depth
depth_df <- tibble(
  subject = 1:54,
  depth   = depth_mbd
) |> arrange(desc(depth))

# Assign layers: median (top 1), central 50%, outer, outliers
girls_df <- as.data.frame(t(girls)) |>
  setNames(paste0("age_", round(ages, 1))) |>
  mutate(
    subject = 1:54,
    depth   = depth_mbd,
    layer   = case_when(
      rank(-depth) == 1        ~ "Functional median",
      rank(-depth) <= 27       ~ "Central 50%",
      depth > quantile(depth_mbd, 0.1) ~ "Outer",
      TRUE                     ~ "Outlier"
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("age_"),
               names_to = "age_str", values_to = "height") |>
  mutate(age = as.numeric(str_remove(age_str, "age_")))

ggplot(girls_df |> filter(layer != "Functional median"),
       aes(age, height, group = subject, color = layer, alpha = layer)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = girls_df |> filter(layer == "Functional median"),
            aes(age, height, group = subject),
            color = "#0f1f3d", linewidth = 2.2, alpha = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Central 50%" = "#2a9d8f",
               "Outer"       = "#e9c46a",
               "Outlier"     = "#e63946"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_alpha_manual(
    values = c("Central 50%" = 0.5,
               "Outer"       = 0.4,
               "Outlier"     = 0.9),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 17, y = 148,
           label = "Functional\nmedian", color = "#0f1f3d",
           fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  labs(title    = "Functional depth — Berkeley Growth Study",
       subtitle = "Modified Band Depth (Lopez-Pintado & Romo, 2009)",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Functional depth is one of the most elegant ideas in FDA. It solves a
fundamental problem: in R you can always rank observations (smallest to
largest) and define medians and quantiles. In function spaces, there is
no natural ordering — a curve cannot be "smaller" or "larger" than another
in any obvious sense.

Depth provides a center-outward ordering. The deepest curve is the
functional median — the most central observation. Curves with low depth
are outliers — they lie far from the bulk of the data.

Modified Band Depth (MBD) has a beautiful geometric interpretation: it
measures the proportion of time that a curve lies within the band formed
by any pair of other curves. If x_i always lies between other curves, it
has high depth. If it often lies outside, it has low depth.

The functional boxplot (Sun & Genton 2011) uses MBD depth to construct
the functional analogue of a box plot: the central region (deepest 50%),
the functional median, whiskers, and outlier flags. It is implemented in
the R package rainbow and fda.usc.


**Applications:**
- **Functional median**: deepest curve
- **Functional boxplot** *(Sun & Genton, 2011)*
- **Outlier detection**: curves with depth below a threshold


Key references: Lopez-Pintado & Romo (2009), JASA; Sun & Genton (2011),
Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics.

If asked about robustness: depth-based methods are naturally robust
to outliers because the median is not sensitive to extreme values.


:::


---

## Functional Depth for biomedical Data

> Which parts of the domain drive the difference between two groups?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}

**López-Pintado & Kun (2021). *Statistics in Medicine*, 40(7), 1639–1652.**

Standard functional tests (FANOVA, permutation) give a **global p-value** — they tell you *whether* two groups differ, but not *where* in the domain the difference lies.

**The depth-based global envelope test:**

1. Rank all curves by **Modified Band Depth** within each group
2. Compute the pointwise difference between group **functional medians**
3. Build a **simultaneous confidence envelope** under $H_0$ via permutation of depth ranks
4. The envelope identifies **exactly which portions** of the domain drive the rejection



:::

:::

::: {.column width="52%"}

```{r fig-envelope-test}
#| fig-height: 8

set.seed(42)
library(fda)
library(fda.usc)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

# ── Simulate two groups of growth curves ─────────────────────────────────────
# Normal birth weight vs low birth weight (inspired by paper application)
ages_env <- seq(0, 18, length.out = 50)
n1 <- 30   # normal birth weight
n2 <- 25   # low birth weight

sim_growth <- function(n, offset_early, offset_late, sd_noise = 3) {
  sapply(1:n, function(i) {
    base  <- 50 + rnorm(1, 0, 2)
    early <- offset_early + rnorm(1, 0, 1)
    late  <- offset_late  + rnorm(1, 0, 1)
    base +
      early * (1 - exp(-0.3 * ages_env)) * 30 +
      late  * pnorm(ages_env, 13, 2) * 20 +
      rnorm(length(ages_env), 0, sd_noise)
  })
}

g1 <- sim_growth(n1, offset_early = 1.0, offset_late = 1.0)  # normal
g2 <- sim_growth(n2, offset_early = 0.7, offset_late = 0.8)  # low BW

# MBD depth within each group
fd1 <- fdata(t(g1), argvals = ages_env)
fd2 <- fdata(t(g2), argvals = ages_env)

dep1 <- depth.mode(fd1)$dep
dep2 <- depth.mode(fd2)$dep

# Functional medians (deepest curve)
med1 <- g1[, which.max(dep1)]
med2 <- g2[, which.max(dep2)]

# Permutation envelope under H0
B <- 499
all_curves <- cbind(g1, g2)
n_all <- ncol(all_curves)
obs_diff <- med1 - med2

perm_diffs <- replicate(B, {
  perm  <- sample(n_all)
  pg1   <- all_curves[, perm[1:n1]]
  pg2   <- all_curves[, perm[(n1+1):n_all]]
  fd_p1 <- fdata(t(pg1), argvals = ages_env)
  fd_p2 <- fdata(t(pg2), argvals = ages_env)
  dp1   <- depth.mode(fd_p1)$dep
  dp2   <- depth.mode(fd_p2)$dep
  pg1[, which.max(dp1)] - pg2[, which.max(dp2)]
})

# 95% simultaneous envelope
env_lower <- apply(perm_diffs, 1, quantile, 0.025)
env_upper <- apply(perm_diffs, 1, quantile, 0.975)

# Identify significant regions
sig_region <- obs_diff < env_lower | obs_diff > env_upper

env_df <- tibble(
  age      = ages_env,
  diff     = obs_diff,
  lower    = env_lower,
  upper    = env_upper,
  sig      = sig_region
)

# ── Panel 1: raw curves ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
raw_df <- bind_rows(
  as.data.frame(g1) |>
    setNames(paste0("s", 1:n1)) |>
    mutate(age = ages_env) |>
    pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "id", values_to = "height") |>
    mutate(group = "Normal birth weight"),
  as.data.frame(g2) |>
    setNames(paste0("s", 1:n2)) |>
    mutate(age = ages_env) |>
    pivot_longer(-age, names_to = "id", values_to = "height") |>
    mutate(group = "Low birth weight")
)

p1 <- ggplot(raw_df, aes(age, height, group = id, color = group)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(age = ages_env, height = med1),
            aes(age, height), color = "#2a9d8f",
            linewidth = 1.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(age = ages_env, height = med2),
            aes(age, height), color = "#e63946",
            linewidth = 1.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Normal birth weight" = "#2a9d8f",
                                 "Low birth weight"    = "#e63946"),
                     name = NULL) +
  labs(title    = "Growth curves by birth weight",
       subtitle = "Bold = functional median (deepest curve by MBD)",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# ── Panel 2: envelope test ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
p2 <- ggplot(env_df, aes(age, diff)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
              fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_point(data = env_df |> filter(sig),
             aes(age, diff), color = "#e63946", size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 15, y = max(env_df$upper) * 0.85,
           label = "95% envelope\nunder H\u2080",
           color = "grey50", size = 3.5, hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = min(env_df$diff) * 0.8,
           label = "Significant\nregion",
           color = "#e63946", size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title    = "Depth-based envelope test",
    subtitle = "Difference of functional medians — red = outside envelope",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = expression(hat(m)[1](t) - hat(m)[2](t))
  ) +
  theme_fda()

p1 | p2
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Lopez-Pintado & Kun (2021) Statistics in Medicine. Key advantage over global tests: the envelope tells you WHERE the difference lies, not just whether it exists. In the birth weight application, the envelope reveals that low birth weight children diverge from normal birth weight children most strongly during early childhood and again around puberty — not uniformly across the growth trajectory. In the PET imaging application, the envelope localizes which brain regions have significantly different receptor binding potential between depressed patients and healthy controls. Note: Sara Lopez-Pintado is Associate Professor of Health Sciences at Northeastern University — same institution as this visiting position.

**Two biomedical applications**

- **Birth weight:** do normal and low birth weight children have different **growth trajectory shapes**? The envelope reveals the specific ages where curves diverge.

- **Brain PET imaging:** do severe depression patients and healthy controls differ in **receptor binding potential**? The envelope localises the brain regions responsible.
:::

---

## Functional Clustering/Classification

> Can we group curves by their shape?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}

**Goal:** identify subjects with similar functional profiles.

::: {.fragment}

**Main approaches:**

**1. FPCA + standard clustering**
Reduce each curve to $K$ scores $(\xi_{i1}, \ldots, \xi_{iK})$, then apply $k$-means, hierarchical clustering, or GMM in $\mathbb{R}^K$.

:::

::: {.fragment}

**2. Model-based functional clustering**
Assume each cluster $g$ has its own mean function $\mu_g(t)$ and covariance structure. Fit via EM algorithm.

:::

::: {.fragment}

**3. $k$-means on functions**
Minimize total within-cluster $L^2$ distance $\min \sum_{g=1}^G \sum_{i:~z_i=g} \|x_i - \mu_g\|_{L^2}^2$

:::

::: {.fragment}

**Classification** follows the same logic — once curves are represented as score vectors or basis coefficients, standard classifiers (LDA, SVM, random forests) apply directly in score space.

:::

:::

:::

::: {.column width="52%"}

```{r fig-clustering}
#| fig-height: 8

data("growth")
ages  <- growth$age
girls <- growth$hgtf
boys  <- growth$hgtm

# Smooth all curves
all_curves <- cbind(girls, boys)
n_all      <- ncol(all_curves)
true_sex   <- c(rep("Female", 54), rep("Male", 39))

bs_all  <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = range(ages), nbasis = 15, norder = 4)
fdpar_all <- fdPar(bs_all, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-1)
all_fd    <- smooth.basis(ages, all_curves, fdpar_all)$fd

# FPCA
fpca_all <- pca.fd(all_fd, nharm = 3)
scores_all <- as.data.frame(fpca_all$scores[, 1:3]) |>
  setNames(paste0("PC", 1:3)) |>
  mutate(sex = true_sex,
         subject = 1:n_all)

# k-means with k=2 on first 2 PCs
set.seed(42)
km_res <- kmeans(scores_all[, c("PC1", "PC2")], centers = 2, nstart = 20)
scores_all$cluster <- factor(km_res$cluster)

# Agreement with true sex
tab <- table(scores_all$cluster, scores_all$sex)
accuracy <- max(sum(diag(tab)), sum(tab) - sum(diag(tab))) / sum(tab)

p1 <- ggplot(scores_all, aes(PC1, PC2, color = sex, shape = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#e63946", "#1e3a5f"), name = "True sex") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17), name = "k-means cluster") +
  labs(title    = "FPCA scores: k-means clustering (k=2)",
       subtitle = paste0("Accuracy vs true sex: ", round(accuracy * 100, 1), "%"),
       x = paste0("PC1 (", round(fpca_all$varprop[1]*100, 1), "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", round(fpca_all$varprop[2]*100, 1), "%)")) +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.box = "vertical")

# Mean curves per cluster
cluster_means <- map_dfr(1:2, function(g) {
  idx <- which(km_res$cluster == g)
  tibble(age   = ages,
         mu    = rowMeans(all_curves[, idx]),
         cluster = paste0("Cluster ", g))
})

p2 <- ggplot(cluster_means, aes(age, mu, color = cluster)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#e63946", "#1e3a5f"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title    = "Cluster mean functions",
       subtitle = "k-means recovers sex structure from curve shape alone",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p1 | p2
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Functional clustering is one of the most immediately useful tools for
clinical researchers: it asks "are there subtypes in this population,
defined by the shape of their trajectories?"

The FPCA + k-means approach is by far the most common in practice
because it is simple, fast, and produces interpretable results.
The score plot gives you a visual representation of the cluster
structure, and the cluster mean functions give you a direct
interpretation of what each cluster looks like in the original
functional space.

The example here uses the Berkeley Growth Study: without knowing
sex labels, k-means on the first two FPCA scores recovers the
sex structure with high accuracy. This demonstrates that the shape
of growth curves alone contains enough information to distinguish
males from females — and that FPCA successfully extracts this
information.

For classification (supervised), the scores feed directly into LDA,
SVM, or random forests. The functional structure is captured by FPCA;
the classification is then a standard multivariate problem.

Key references: James & Sugar (2003), JASA; Giacofci et al. (2013),
Biometrics; Jacques & Preda (2014), Statistics and Computing.

The canonical classification example in Ramsay & Silverman is exactly the Tecator spectrometry dataset — classifying meat samples as high vs low fat content from their NIR absorbance curves. It is the go-to example because it demonstrates that classifying directly in the functional space outperforms classifying from scalar summaries.
The classic R&S pipeline is:
- Smooth the absorbance curves
- compute the second derivative 
- Run FPCA on the second derivatives
- Classify with LDA in the score space

Note on alignment: before clustering, if curves have phase variation
(e.g., the pubertal growth spurt occurs at different ages in different
children), registration/alignment should be applied first. Clustering
unregistered curves conflates amplitude variation with phase variation
and can produce spurious clusters.
:::

---

## Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM)

> The shape of your glucose curve matters more than your average.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}

::: {style="font-size: 78%;"}

**Setting:** CGM devices record glucose every 5 minutes — 288 observations per day per patient. Standard summaries: HbA1c, mean glucose, time-in-range.

**What FDA adds:**

- The **daily glucose profile** $x_i(t)$ is the unit of observation — a curve over 24 hours
- **FPCA** reveals phenotypes: flat controllers vs reactive spikers vs nocturnal hypoglycaemics
- **Functional regression**: predict HbA1c or cardiovascular risk from the entire profile, not just mean glucose
- **Functional clustering**: identify patient subtypes with similar glucose dynamics for personalised treatment

**Key reference**: Matabuena et al. (2022). *Glucodensities: a new representation of glucose profiles using distributional data analysis.* Statistical Methods in Medical Research.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="52%"}

```{r fig-cgm}
#| fig-height: 8

set.seed(123)
hours   <- seq(0, 24, length.out = 288)
n_pat   <- 60

# Simulate 3 CGM phenotypes
sim_cgm <- function(i) {
  type <- sample(c("flat", "spiker", "nocturnal"), 1,
                 prob = c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2))
  base <- 100 + rnorm(1, 0, 10)
  if (type == "flat") {
    base + 10*sin(2*pi*hours/24) + rnorm(288, 0, 5)
  } else if (type == "spiker") {
    base +
      40*dnorm(hours, 8,  0.8)*15 +
      50*dnorm(hours, 13, 0.8)*15 +
      35*dnorm(hours, 19, 0.8)*15 +
      rnorm(288, 0, 8)
  } else {
    base - 25*dnorm(hours, 3, 1.5)*8 +
      15*sin(2*pi*hours/24) + rnorm(288, 0, 6)
  }
}

cgm_mat <- sapply(1:n_pat, sim_cgm)

# Smooth
bs_cgm  <- fda::create.bspline.basis(rangeval = c(0,24), nbasis = 25, norder = 4)
fdp_cgm <- fda::fdPar(bs_cgm, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e-1)
cgm_fd  <- fda::smooth.basis(hours, cgm_mat, fdp_cgm)$fd

# FPCA
fpca_cgm <- fda::pca.fd(cgm_fd, nharm = 3)
pve_cgm  <- round(fpca_cgm$varprop * 100, 1)

mu_cgm  <- as.numeric(fda::eval.fd(hours, fda::mean.fd(cgm_fd)))
efuns_c <- fda::eval.fd(hours, fpca_cgm$harmonics)

# Select 3 contrasting subjects
scores_c <- fpca_cgm$scores
idx1 <- which.max(scores_c[, 1])
idx2 <- which.min(scores_c[, 1])
idx3 <- which.max(scores_c[, 2])

sel_df <- map_dfr(list(
  list(idx = idx1, lab = "High PC1"),
  list(idx = idx2, lab = "Low PC1"),
  list(idx = idx3, lab = "High PC2")
), function(x) {
  tibble(hour = hours,
         glucose = cgm_mat[, x$idx],
         phenotype = x$lab)
})

ggplot(
  as.data.frame(cgm_mat[, sample(1:n_pat, 25)]) |>
    setNames(paste0("p", 1:25)) |>
    mutate(hour = hours) |>
    pivot_longer(-hour, names_to = "id", values_to = "glucose"),
  aes(hour, glucose, group = id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15, color = "#1e3a5f", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = sel_df,
            aes(hour, glucose, color = phenotype, group = phenotype),
            linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(hour = hours, glucose = mu_cgm),
            aes(hour, glucose), color = "#0f1f3d",
            linewidth = 1.8, linetype = "dashed",
            inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("High PC1" = "#e63946",
               "Low PC1"  = "#2a9d8f",
               "High PC2" = "#e9c46a"),
    name = "Phenotype"
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(70, 180), linetype = "dotted",
             color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 23, y = 72,  label = "Hypo threshold (70)",
           size = 3, color = "grey40", hjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 23, y = 182, label = "Hyper threshold (180)",
           size = 3, color = "grey40", hjust = 1) +
  labs(title    = "CGM daily glucose profiles",
       subtitle = paste0("60 simulated patients — dashed = mean curve — FPCA PC1: ",
                         pve_cgm[1], "%, PC2: ", pve_cgm[2], "%"),
       x = "Hour of day", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
CGM is one of the most exciting applications of FDA in clinical biostatistics. The device generates a genuine functional observation — 288 glucose values per day — and the clinical question is inherently about the shape of the curve, not just its mean. Standard summaries like HbA1c or time-in-range discard phenotypic information that FDA can recover. Matabuena et al. (2022) proposed glucodensities as a distributional representation of CGM data, which is a related functional approach.
:::

---

## EEG Spectral Curves in Epilepsy

> The frequency profile of a brain signal is a functional observation.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}

::: {style="font-size: 78%;"}

**Setting:** EEG recordings decomposed into **power spectral density** curves — power as a function of frequency (0-50 Hz). One curve per epoch per patient.

**Standard approach:** summarize to band power (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma) — 5 scalar values per epoch.

**What FDA adds:**

- The **full spectral curve** $x_i(\omega)$ preserves shape information within and between bands
- **FPCA** on spectral curves identifies modes of spectral variation linked to seizure onset, sleep stages, or drug response
- **Functional classification**: distinguish pre-ictal from inter-ictal periods directly from the spectral curve shape
- **Scalar-on-function regression**: predict seizure probability from the entire spectral profile

**Key reference:**: Ombao et al. (2001). *SLEX Analysis of Multivariate Nonstationary Time Series.* JASA.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="52%"}

```{r fig-eeg-spectra}
#| fig-height: 5.5

set.seed(77)
freqs   <- seq(1, 50, length.out = 200)
n_eeg   <- 50

# Simulate spectral curves: interictal vs preictal
sim_spectrum <- function(state) {
  base  <- 20 * exp(-0.08 * freqs)
  alpha <- if (state == "interictal")
             15 * dnorm(freqs, 10, 1.5) * 10
           else
             8  * dnorm(freqs, 10, 1.5) * 10
  theta <- if (state == "preictal")
             12 * dnorm(freqs, 6, 1.2) * 10
           else
             5  * dnorm(freqs, 6, 1.2) * 10
  gamma <- if (state == "preictal")
             6  * dnorm(freqs, 40, 3) * 10
           else
             2  * dnorm(freqs, 40, 3) * 10
  pmax(base + alpha + theta + gamma + rnorm(200, 0, 1), 0)
}

n_ii <- 30; n_pi <- 20
spec_mat <- cbind(
  sapply(1:n_ii, function(i) sim_spectrum("interictal")),
  sapply(1:n_pi, function(i) sim_spectrum("preictal"))
)
labels_eeg <- c(rep("Inter-ictal", n_ii), rep("Pre-ictal", n_pi))

mu_ii <- rowMeans(spec_mat[, 1:n_ii])
mu_pi <- rowMeans(spec_mat[, (n_ii+1):(n_ii+n_pi)])

# Band boundaries
bands <- tibble(
  xmin  = c(1, 4, 8, 13, 30),
  xmax  = c(4, 8, 13, 30, 50),
  label = c("δ", "θ", "α", "β", "γ"),
  fill  = c("#e9c46a","#f4a261","#e76f51","#2a9d8f","#457b9d")
)

eeg_df <- as.data.frame(spec_mat[, c(1:5, (n_ii+1):(n_ii+5))]) |>
  setNames(c(paste0("ii_", 1:5), paste0("pi_", 1:5))) |>
  mutate(freq = freqs) |>
  pivot_longer(-freq, names_to = "id", values_to = "power") |>
  mutate(state = ifelse(startsWith(id, "ii"), "Inter-ictal", "Pre-ictal"))

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = bands,
            aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = label),
            alpha = 0.08, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(bands$fill, bands$label),
                    name = "Band") +
  geom_line(data = eeg_df,
            aes(freq, power, group = id, color = state),
            alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(freq = freqs, power = mu_ii, state = "Inter-ictal"),
            aes(freq, power, color = state), linewidth = 1.8) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(freq = freqs, power = mu_pi, state = "Pre-ictal"),
            aes(freq, power, color = state), linewidth = 1.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Inter-ictal" = "#2a9d8f",
                                 "Pre-ictal"   = "#e63946"),
                     name = "State") +
  labs(title    = "EEG power spectral density curves",
       subtitle = "Pre-ictal vs inter-ictal — mean curves in bold",
       x = "Frequency (Hz)", y = "Power (μV²/Hz)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.box = "vertical")
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
EEG spectra are natural functional observations — power as a function of frequency. The standard approach of summarizing to 5 band-power values loses information about the shape within and between bands. FDA treats the entire spectral curve as one observation. This is particularly powerful for seizure prediction: pre-ictal spectral curves have a distinctive shape (elevated theta, suppressed alpha, elevated gamma) that is visible in the mean curve difference but also in FPCA modes of variation.
:::

---

## Survival Analysis with Functional Predictors

> Can the shape of a longitudinal biomarker predict time to event?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {style="font-size: 77%;"}

**Setting:** patients followed until death or censoring. For each patient, a longitudinal biomarker curve $x_i(t)$ is observed (PSA, creatinine, CD4...).

**Standard approach:** include the last observed value, the slope, or the AUC as a scalar covariate in a Cox model.

**FDA approach — functional Cox model:**

$$\lambda_i(s) = \lambda_0(s) \exp\left(\int_T x_i(t)\,\beta(t)\,dt\right)$$

The log-hazard ratio is a **scalar-on-function regression** on the entire biomarker trajectory. The coefficient function $\beta(t)$ tells you **which parts of the trajectory** are most prognostic.

**Key advantage:** $\beta(t)$ may reveal that the trajectory shape over a specific time window — not the overall level — is the clinically relevant predictor.

**Reference:** Gellar et al. (2015). *Cox regression models with functional covariates for survival data.* Statistical Modelling.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r fig-survival-fda}
#| fig-height: 9

library(survival)
library(fda)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

# ── PBC longitudinal data ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# pbcseq: repeated bilirubin measurements per patient
# pbc:    survival outcome (time, status)
data("pbcseq", package = "survival")
data("pbc",    package = "survival")

# Patients with at least 6 measurements and known outcome
pbc_surv <- pbc |>
  filter(!is.na(status)) |>
  mutate(dead = as.integer(status == 2)) |>
  select(id, time, dead)

# Keep patients with >= 6 longitudinal bilirubin measurements
ids_ok <- pbcseq |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  filter(n >= 6) |>
  pull(id)

pbcseq_filt <- pbcseq |>
  filter(id %in% ids_ok) |>
  inner_join(pbc_surv, by = "id") |>
  filter(day <= time)   # only measurements before event

# Interpolate each patient's bilirubin onto a common grid (0-3000 days)
t_common <- seq(0, 3000, length.out = 60)
n_pat    <- length(unique(pbcseq_filt$id))
ids_use  <- unique(pbcseq_filt$id)

bili_mat <- matrix(NA, nrow = 60, ncol = length(ids_use))
surv_vec <- numeric(length(ids_use))
dead_vec <- integer(length(ids_use))

for (k in seq_along(ids_use)) {
  pid   <- ids_use[k]
  df_k  <- pbcseq_filt |> filter(id == pid) |> arrange(day)
  # interpolate log-bilirubin onto common grid
  approx_k <- approx(df_k$day, log(df_k$bili + 1),
                     xout = t_common, rule = 2)$y
  bili_mat[, k] <- approx_k
  surv_vec[k]   <- pbc_surv$time[pbc_surv$id == pid]
  dead_vec[k]   <- pbc_surv$dead[pbc_surv$id == pid]
}

# Smooth each patient's trajectory
bs_pbc  <- create.bspline.basis(rangeval = range(t_common),
                                 nbasis = 15, norder = 4)
fdp_pbc <- fdPar(bs_pbc, Lfdobj = 2, lambda = 1e0)
bili_fd <- smooth.basis(t_common, bili_mat, fdp_pbc)$fd

# FPCA
fpca_pbc <- pca.fd(bili_fd, nharm = 4)
pve_pbc  <- round(fpca_pbc$varprop * 100, 1)

mu_bili  <- as.numeric(eval.fd(t_common, mean.fd(bili_fd)))

# ── Panel 1: bilirubin trajectories by outcome ────────────────────────────────
# Select 8 dead and 8 alive patients
idx_dead  <- which(dead_vec == 1)[1:8]
idx_alive <- which(dead_vec == 0)[1:8]
idx_sel   <- c(idx_dead, idx_alive)

traj_df <- map_dfr(idx_sel, function(k) {
  tibble(
    day     = t_common,
    logbili = bili_mat[, k],
    id      = k,
    outcome = ifelse(dead_vec[k] == 1, "Dead", "Alive/censored")
  )
})

p1 <- ggplot(traj_df, aes(day, logbili, group = id, color = outcome)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.55, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Dead"             = "#e63946",
                                 "Alive/censored"   = "#2a9d8f"),
                     name = NULL) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(day = t_common, logbili = mu_bili),
            aes(day, logbili), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            color = "#0f1f3d", linewidth = 1.6, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 2800, y = 0.6,
           label = "μ(t)", color = "#0f1f3d",
           fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  labs(title    = "Log-bilirubin trajectories — PBC study",
       subtitle = "Red = died, Green = alive/censored. Dashed = mean curve.",
       x = "Days since enrolment", y = "log(bilirubin + 1)") +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# ── Panel 2: FPCA scree + PC1 scores vs survival ─────────────────────────────
scores_pbc <- fpca_pbc$scores[, 1]

surv_df <- tibble(
  pc1     = scores_pbc,
  surv    = surv_vec,
  outcome = ifelse(dead_vec == 1, "Dead", "Alive/censored")
)

p2 <- ggplot(surv_df, aes(pc1, surv, color = outcome)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1,
              aes(group = 1), color = "#0f1f3d") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Dead"           = "#e63946",
                                 "Alive/censored" = "#2a9d8f"),
                     name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title    = paste0("PC1 score (", pve_pbc[1], "% var) vs survival time"),
    subtitle = "Higher PC1 = more elevated bilirubin trajectory = shorter survival",
    x = "PC1 score", y = "Survival time (days)"
  ) +
  theme_fda() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p1 | p2
```

:::
:::

::: {.notes}

Real data: survival::pbcseq from R — 312 PBC patients with repeated serum bilirubin measurements and survival outcome (death or liver transplant). Methodology: Gellar et al. (2015), Statistical Modelling — functional Cox model where the entire bilirubin trajectory is the predictor. Left panel: patients who died tend to have rising bilirubin trajectories; survivors stay low. Right panel: PC1 of the bilirubin functional data captures most variance and correlates negatively with survival time — patients with higher bilirubin profiles (high PC1) die sooner. The functional Cox model uses the whole trajectory beta(t), not just the last value or the slope — it reveals which time windows of bilirubin elevation are most prognostic.

PBC = Primary Biliary Cholangitis — a chronic autoimmune liver disease where bile ducts are progressively destroyed. Bilirubin is the primary marker of liver function decline. This is a canonical dataset in survival analysis, also used in joint modelling literature.

The functional Cox model is a powerful extension of survival analysis. Instead of reducing the biomarker trajectory to a scalar (last value, slope, AUC), the model uses the entire trajectory as a functional predictor. The coefficient function beta(t) reveals which time windows are most prognostic — for example, it may show that the rate of PSA change in the last 6 months before censoring is far more predictive of survival than the overall PSA level. This has direct clinical implications for monitoring frequency and timing.
:::



# R Ecosystem for FDA {background-color="#1e3a5f"}

Key packages and resources

---

## R Packages for FDA

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

### Core FDA

**`fda`** *(Ramsay, Graves, Hooker)*  
The foundational package. Basis systems, smoothing, FPCA, functional regression, registration.


**`fda.usc`** *(Febrero-Bande & Oviedo de la Fuente)*  
Functional statistics: depth measures, outlier detection, classification, regression.


**`refund`** *(Goldsmith, Scheipl, Huang et al.)*  
Regression with functional data: scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, function-on-function via penalized splines.


**`goffda`** *(García-Portugués, Álvarez-Liébana et al.)*  
Goodness-of-Fit tests for Functional Data

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Extended Toolkit


**`wavethresh`** *(Nason)*  
Wavelet-based functional smoothing and decomposition.

**`ftsa`** *(Hyndman & Shang)*  
Functional time series — forecasting, decomposition.

**`rainbow`** *(Hyndman & Shang)*  
Functional data visualization and depth-based methods.

**`tidyfun`** *(Scheipl, Goldsmith & Wrobel)*  
Tidy Functional Data


:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The R ecosystem for FDA is mature and well-maintained. The fda package
by Ramsay et al. is the foundational reference implementation —
everything in the Ramsay & Silverman textbook is implemented there.

refund is the most actively developed package for functional regression,
with interfaces to mgcv for penalized splines and support for all three
regression paradigms (SoF, FoS, FoF).

fdapace is essential for sparse and irregular data — it implements the
PACE methodology of Yao, Muller & Wang (2005) and handles the case
where different subjects have different measurement times and numbers
of observations.

fda.usc is particularly strong for exploratory analysis: depth measures,
functional boxplots, outlier detection, and nonparametric classification.

For Python users, scikit-fda has been growing rapidly and now covers
most of the basics — basis smoothing, FPCA, functional regression,
depth measures — with a sklearn-compatible API.
:::

---

## Key References

::: {style="font-size: 78%;"}

**Foundational textbooks**

- Ramsay, J.O. & Silverman, B.W. (2005). *Functional Data Analysis* (2nd ed.). Springer. ← **Start here**
- Ramsay, J.O., Hooker, G. & Graves, S. (2009). *Functional Data Analysis with R and MATLAB*. Springer.
- Hsing, T. & Eubank, R. (2015). *Theoretical Foundations of Functional Data Analysis*. Wiley.
- Kokoszka, P. & Reimherr, M. (2017). *Introduction to Functional Data Analysis*. CRC Press.

**Key papers**

- Ramsay, J.O. & Dalzell, C.J. (1991). Some tools for functional data analysis. *JRSS-B*, 53, 539-572. ← term coined here
- Yao, F., Muller, H.G. & Wang, J.L. (2005). Functional data analysis for sparse longitudinal data. *JASA*, 100, 577-590. ← PACE
- Lopez-Pintado, S. & Romo, J. (2009). On the concept of depth for functional data. *JASA*, 104, 718-734. ← depth
- Leroux, A. et al. (2019). Organizing and analyzing the activity data in NHANES. *Statistics in Biosciences*, 11, 262-287.
- Wang, J.L., Chiou, J.M. & Muller, H.G. (2016). Functional data analysis. *Annual Review of Statistics*, 3, 257-295. ← **best review paper**

:::

::: {.notes}
If you give one reference to take away, it should be Wang, Chiou &
Muller (2016) in Annual Review of Statistics — it is the most accessible
and comprehensive review of the field, covering the main methodological
directions with practical guidance.

For textbooks, Ramsay & Silverman (2005) is the classic reference.
Kokoszka & Reimherr (2017) is more theoretically oriented and is a
good companion for those who want the mathematical foundations.

For applications in health sciences specifically, the NHANES
accelerometry papers (Leroux, Goldsmith et al.) provide excellent
worked examples of FDA applied to real wearable sensor data.
:::
